Sports.title: Tielemans: I did not expect to leave Aston Villa for Man Utd this summer
Sports.content:
'Not really, no' - the perhaps surprising answer from Manchester United’s summer signing Youri Tielemans when asked whether he expected to leave his former club Aston Villa in this window.

It is easy to forget Man Utd swiftly and covertly signed a player with eight years of Premier League experience at what feels like the height of his footballing powers due to a generous release clause of just £35m.

In his first interview since joining the club, Tielemans has opened up about just how the move came around, especially having been of interest to Manchester United on a few occasions in the past as well.

"There has been two times that I spoke with the club, but it did not achieve anything so I was just very calm about it," Tielemans said.

"It was mainly my agent that was dealing with it, I was more so focused on the World Cup which was a big thing for me. When it was time that it was accepted and acceptable, I would say then I was made aware.

Image: Tielemans signed a five-year deal with Man Utd

"I was not expecting much [a summer move], to be fair. I was just focused on my football, focused on the World Cup, trying to perform as best as I could for my country. Then every summer something can happen."

Tielemans joined Villa as a free agent after leaving Leicester when they were relegated to the Championship. For some reason, a move to the conventional 'top six' never seemed rumoured or close during his time at either of his previous clubs - which is why his move to Manchester United was deemed a surprise.

But did he think the opportunity had passed him by? "Not really, because I know that at Villa we did amazing things," Tielemans explained.

Image: Tielemans made his first appearance for Man Utd against PSG

"We achieved the Europa League win which was great for the club but there are still clubs above Aston Villa, and Manchester United is one of them.

"Especially at this moment, there is a very positive mood in and around the club so I am just hopeful that we can have a great story together.

"Aston Villa is a great club and I owe them the world. They have put me back at my best level so I am very thankful."

Reuniting with Evans and Rashford

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo were among more Manchester United players returning for pre-season training.

Although Tielemans is still getting used to his new surroundings, he will have felt at ease knowing one member of staff very well in particular - Jonny Evans.

The former centre-back spent four and a half years with Tielemans at Leicester and is now a key member of Michael Carrick's backroom staff.

When I asked just how nice it felt to be reunited with his former team-mate, he couldn't resist a huge smile.

Image: Jonny Evans played with Tielemans at Leicester, and is now a coach at Man Utd

"Jonny has always been a main character," Tielemans said. "He has always been trying to educate young players and he welcomed me at Leicester and now here.

"It is a bit weird to see him as a staff member to be honest, but it is going great and he knows me, he knows what I need and what I can bring to the team so it helps me as well."

Another relatively new team-mate Tielemans spent slightly less time with was Marcus Rashford. The pair spent six months together when the England international was on loan at Aston Villa for the second half of the 2024/25 season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player With Marcus Rashford being fully reintegrated into the Manchester United squad after his loan at Barcelona came to an end earlier this summer, Sky Sports News' Danyal Khan explains how the England forward's return can benefit the club.

There is a lot of attention on the Man Utd winger's return to the club as well as what he can offer this team, Tielemans only has fond memories of their time at Villa Park together and is looking forward to more of them.

He said: "He was great. There had been so much talk about him and bringing pressure with the media around him, but I thought he was just so good.

"He was very humble, he was hard working and from the first training session, you could tell, his touch, his acceleration was amazing.

"That was just what we needed at the time at Villa as well so he did many good things and hopefully he can bring them here."

World Cup, his injury and Balogun's red card reversal

Image: Tielemans was Belgium's captain at the 2026 World Cup

Tielemans has had an eventful summer, even before his surprise move to Manchester United.

He captained Belgium at this summer's World Cup, who were knocked out in the quarter-finals by eventual winners Spain. Tielemans was unable to play in the quarter-final after picking up an injury in the warm-up, but for any Man Utd fans concerned whether he has any lingering injury concerns, he is more than ready for the new season.

Tielemans said: "It was just an overload of too many games, too many minutes and unfortunately my body could not cope with it anymore.

"We played 120 minutes against Senegal and from there, we had less time in between games. We played the USA three or four days later, then three days after that, we played against Spain. In the warm-up, my body switched off for some reason."

Before his injury, the midfielder played a key role in Belgium's World Cup campaign, scoring two goals in their dramatic win against Senegal in the round of 32.

Image: Belgium beat the USA 4-1 despite the controversy surrounding Folarin Balogun's suspended red card

However, perhaps the most eventful game was their round of 16 tie against the USA. In what proved to be one of the most controversial decisions of the tournament, USA striker Folarin Balogun's red card was suspended for the tie, although in the end it did not matter as Belgium went on to win 4-1.

"Originally we were surprised by the decision to revert the red card and his suspension," Tielemans said.

"Now for us, it did not really change anything other than the preparation leading up to the game because it is a different type of player than the other player that was meant to play.

"Other than that, we were very calm and we just accepted our fate and tried to have a good game."

Sports.title: What next for Birmingham City? Why Davies is changing his approach
Sports.content:
Birmingham City is a football club transformed. Over 20,000 season tickets have been sold for the forthcoming Championship season, with 14,000 more on the waiting list. Fan parks surround St Andrew's these days. The buzz around the place is palpable.

There are grand plans to reconnect England's second city to the club that bears its name, unlocking its true potential. Supporters clubs are springing up around the world, a product of Tom Brady's presence. And all the talk is of trying to be Premier League ready.

Given this context, with an ambitious ownership and a success-starved support, it is understandable if Birmingham are in a hurry. Excitement brings expectation, not just internally but externally. There is the sense of a club going places. But it takes time.

On reflection, maybe last season was a moment for the club to breathe rather than a case of lost momentum. After all, you must go back 14 years to the 2011/12 season, when Birmingham were in Europe, for a better finish than the 10th-place effort of 2025/26.

"It was our first season back, which people found hard to remember at times," Birmingham manager Chris Davies tells Sky Sports ahead of Saturday's season-opener against Sheffield United, live on Sky. He is not talking about the club's supporters - "they have been great" - but everyone. This is a man carrying a lot of hopes and dreams.

"One thing I did learn was that I can handle it," he says. "I can handle the ups and downs." There had not been too many of the latter as Birmingham won the League One title with a record-breaking 111 points, their possession football proving utterly dominant.

Last season was more testing. "You can know about the Championship but to feel it is something different." England's second tier asked different questions. Davies and his team did not always have the answers. Plan A worked only some of the time.

"We came up from League One playing total football, having 80 per cent possession with a lot of circulating the ball, a lot of dominating the ball. It was really effective for us because we just controlled games pretty much the whole way through," he explains.

"In the Championship we were very technical in our recruitment of some smaller players, more technical players, and we tried to use that style. It had really good days and it had days where we just didn't have enough punch, especially away from home."

In that context, opening the season with a hard-fought Carabao Cup win at Swansea in which Birmingham scored the only goal having had 39 per cent of the ball was more than just satisfying. It suggested that his Blues side have added different elements to their game.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Carabao Cup first-round match between Swansea and Birmingham

The scorer, August Priske, is a robust young target-man added in January who looks to have benefited from that half-season in the Championship. The 22-year-old Dane also netted the opening goal against Barcelona in front of a packed St Andrew's last month.

"Jhon Solis, Carlos Vicente and August came in at the same time and that little six months that they did have is their initiation to what English football is like, what the Championship is like, and now they are ready to go. They have all done very well."

Vicente, a combative Spanish winger, provided the assist for Priske's goal at Swansea. Solis also scored against Barcelona with the Colombian already proving a popular figure with the fans. He adds presence to Birmingham's midfield just as Priske does up top.

"When I reflected on the season, I thought for us to take the next step and progress, physicality is going to be really important. The game now is a lot of man-to-man pressing, a lot of set-piece emphasis. You need the physical capacity to deal with it."

That thinking has shaped Birmingham's summer too. Supplementing those winter additions, the club have brought in Dael Fry. The expectation is that a 6ft 4in centre-back with nearly 300 Championship appearances to his name will be able to adapt quickly.

The intention is to add to what Davies has already built, rather than pivot completely. "As a team that can keep the ball, it is a lot easier to then move into a more pragmatic or direct style than being a team that only knows how to play pragmatic or direct football."

That change actually began during the closing weeks of the last campaign. Birmingham were in 17th place in mid-April, but Davies used the brief international break in the spring to make some of these adjustments to their style of play. They went more direct.

Image: Christoph Klarer's passing sonar shows how Birmingham have become more direct

"I started thinking about being a little bit more flexible with the shape we were using and how we were positioning ourselves, but focusing more on more direct play, more transitions and more set-pieces if possible. So we sort of finished the season that way."

Birmingham ended the campaign on a five-game unbeaten run, earning that top-10 finish and taking some belief into the summer.

"It is a fine balance because we don't want to lose what we're good at. What I won't come away from is the pressing. I don't think any team last season in the Championship really played through our press consistently. I thought it was really effective for us."

But there will be tweaks once Birmingham win the ball back. "I think that hopefully is something that we can have as a weapon that we can use a little bit more. When we get the ball, just to go forward that little bit quicker, hopefully win more set-pieces."

That explains another addition behind the scenes. Birmingham have brought in a specialist set-piece coach in Scott Fry, with Davies identifying dead-ball situations as an obvious way that his team can become genuine promotion contenders this season.

Solis scored from one against Barcelona. Priske's winner against Swansea came after a set-piece found Vicente and he squared the ball for the striker. In other words, this emphasis on set-pieces is already making the difference. And Davies has been doing his sums.

"We have a set-piece coach and the idea is to score more from them. We needed to score 70-odd goals really to be in among those top teams last season." Crucially, that was the total hit by the top six but not the rest of the Championship. Birmingham scored 57.

The task this time around is to find those extra 13 goals somehow. "If six or seven of those can come from set-pieces and two or three can come from counter-attacks, then you only need another two or three from your general football. So it is absolutely doable."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jude Bellingham discusses his love of Birmingham and his love of cricket

Absolutely doable. That sums up the mood. Last time, they were learning about the Championship. Now they know. "It was not just me, several players had never played in it before. Now they have 40 games in the bank. They know what it is like away at Millwall."

At the training ground, Davies has tried to strip back the buzzwords that once adorned the walls. No more gimmicks is the mantra now. Leaner and meaner, like the squad. The feeling is that there is more continuity now, that this Birmingham are ready to kick on.

Craig Gardner has left as director of football but the club has played down the impact, leaning on the experienced Mike Rigg. Commercially, Birmingham continue to grow, with the biggest revenue of any Championship club not reliant on parachute money.

After storming up and then stabilising, the next step awaits Birmingham City. And now, it feels like everyone is ready for it. "I am confident that we can keep progressing. That is the big thing," says Davies. "We just need to keep moving forward and getting stronger."

Sports.title: Championship play-off changes, new managers & star players - the EFL is BACK!
Sports.content:
The 2026/27 EFL season is here!

We kick off on Friday night with Wolves vs Blackburn Rovers, and every Championship, League One and League Two game is LIVE this weekend!

But what have we got in store for the new campaign? We take a look at some of the key stories...

Championship

From top six to top eight... a new play-off system has arrived!

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Simeon Gholam explains all you need to know on how the play-offs have changed this season in the Championship

The most significant alteration to domestic football in decades has happened over the summer, with the Championship play-offs expanding from a top-six spot to a top-eight position this season, presenting clubs with more opportunity for promotion.

What has (and hasn't) changed?

1st and 2nd are automatically promoted as normal.

3rd and 4th still qualify for the semi-finals.

5th vs 8th and 6th vs 7th in one-off eliminator ties at the home of the side who finishes higher up the league.

The winners of the eliminator ties progress to the semi-finals, to face 3rd and 4th in two-legged ties with the second leg at the home of the side that finishes higher up the league.

One other key thing to note is that, whatever happens, 3rd will face the lowest-ranked team remaining in the semi-finals. So if 8th beats 5th, and 6th beats 7th in the eliminators, 3rd will face 8th and 4th will face 6th. There is no pre-set path for the semi-finals before the eliminators.

in the semi-finals. So if 8th beats 5th, and 6th beats 7th in the eliminators, 3rd will face 8th and 4th will face 6th. There is no pre-set path for the semi-finals before the eliminators. As per usual, the winners of the two semi-finals meet at Wembley for a place in the Premier League.

Are the relegated clubs automatic favourites?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kevin Nolan and Darren Moore tell the EFL Show why Jarrod Bowen is key for West Ham's hopes for an instant return to the Premier League

It did not take long for West Ham and Wolves to be installed as favourites for an immediate return to the Premier League.

The Hammers are playing at this level for the first time in 14 years, and have kept hold of head coach Nuno Espirito Santo and key asset Jarrod Bowen.

Both are familiar with this level. Nuno won the Championship - with Wolves - in 2018, while Bowen played in it with Hull City before he left for east London.

Wolves, meanwhile, replaced boss Rob Edwards with the relatively unknown quantity of Cesar Peixoto in the summer. But the quality in their squad could prove telling, with Andre, Mateus Mane, Santiago Bueno and Hugo Bueno sticking about.

They have also added Raul Jimenez and Kieran Trippier to the bank. Experience and class.

It is Burnley where a bit more uncertainty lingers. They have appointed a new head coach in Nicky Hayen, a 45-year-old Belgian who has previously managed Club Brugge and Genk.

But it is worth remembering the Clarets have won promotion in their last two Championship seasons - both times with 100+ points. They are experts at this level.

According to the Sky Sports supercomputer, West Ham and Wolves are the two favourites, with Burnley in fourth just behind Middlesbrough...

Middlesbrough go big to try and get over the line

It was some campaign for Middlesbrough last season. They spent more days in the top two than any other club, but managed to finish fifth.

They were then the victim of the Spygate saga, lost to Southampton in the play-off semi-finals, were reinstated to the final, then lost at Wembley to a stoppage-time Oli McBurnie goal for Hull City.

But any potential hangover looks like it has already been left behind with some of their work in the transfer window.

Owner Steve Gibson has taken his chequebook out and spent serious money to strengthen. Striker Will Lankshear has already made his mark with the winning goal against Wrexham in the Carabao Cup. He scored 11 goals for a struggling Oxford side last season and arrives from Spurs.

Sebastian Berhalter comes in, having last been seen playing for the USA at the World Cup, while goalkeeper Radek Vitek from Manchester United is also an eye-catching addition. He impressed on loan at Bristol City last season.

Kim Hellberg and some Boro fans may be wondering where this backing was in January when they were crying out for reinforcements, but it has certainly led to a swell of excitement at the Riverside about what's possible this season.

Can Southampton escape Spygate scandal?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking exclusively to Sky Sports' Mark McAdam before the FA charge, Southampton boss Tonda Eckert revealed the challenges he has faced after the Spygate scandal that resulted in their expulsion from the Championship play-offs

It was the story that dominated the landscape of last season. A shockwave went around the footballing world when Southampton were expelled from the play-offs after their role in the Spygate scandal.

But the club were quick to back Tonda Eckert, and although an FA charge still hangs over the boss, they have tried to move on and heal the wounds caused by the damage.

Fears of a player exodus have been quelled, with only midfielder Shea Charles departing so far, and the club has brought in goalkeeper Daniel Peretz and striker Cyle Larin permanently, after both starred on loan in the second half of last season.

They will have to overcome a four-point deduction. But they came from a long way back last season with a remarkable run in the second half of the campaign, and they certainly have the quality to challenge.

Managerial changes in the Championship

There are also a few other managerial changes to make a note of. Tony Mowbray is back at Blackburn Rovers four years after he left the club, while Watford have brought in Alessio Dionisi.

Elsewhere, Michael Skubala left Lincoln City after leading them to promotion to join Bristol City. While his exit opened the door for the Imps to make the unique move of appointing joint-managers in the role. Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw take the reins at Sincil Bank.

League One

Will Leicester turn things around?

Image: Leicester City manager Russell Martin

For just the second time in their history, and just 10 years after they won the Premier League title, Leicester City have found themselves in League One.

Russell Martin has taken the helm, as they look to end a miserable run of back-to-back relegations. He also has work to do in winning over some doubters, after miserable ends to his spells at Southampton and Rangers in his last two roles.

The addition of experience has been the aim of the summer, with the likes of Liam Cullen, Conor Chaplin and Wes Burns already joining.

A new dawn for Wednesday and who else could compete for promotion?

The Chansiri era is finally over at Sheffield Wednesday, and there has been a swirl of optimism around the club under new owner David Storch, despite relegation.

Henrik Pedersen, who led the Owls through the grim 2025/26 season, has been given the opportunity to see if he can get more out of a squad that is actually built to compete.

Louie Barry is an eye-catching addition. Injuries have blighted his progress but he has shown what a star he can be at this level for Stockport County, while Barry Bannan is back home after his stint at Millwall.

Luton are quite fancied under Jack Wilshere after a positive run in the second half of last season.

As are Plymouth Argyle, who have been exceptional so far in 2026, just missing out on the play-offs.

Managerial changes in League One

Image: Aaron Ramsey has taken his first permanent managerial role at Oxford United

There has been a particularly notable appointment at Oxford United, with Aaron Ramsey taking his first permanent managerial role to replace Matt Bloomfield, who surprisingly departed in the summer.

It has not been an easy start for Ramsey, however, as he has already had to deal with a transfer embargo which has left him unable to make any additions at the relegated club.

Elsewhere, Daniel Stendel has returned to Barnsley, Martin Drury has taken charge at Huddersfield Town and Jimmy McNulty left Rochdale to join Stockport following the departure of Dave Challinor.

Bromley's first season in the third tier!

Bromley were promoted to the EFL for the first time in their history in 2024, and it took just two seasons for them to seal promotion from League Two.

The Ravens won the title last season, and will now compete in the third tier of English football for the first time. It has only been 11 years since they were promoted to the National League for the first time.

They have been installed as the favourites for relegation, but Andy Woodman's side have defied the critics before and will be keen to do so again. Don't rule out anything at Hayes Lane.

All change at York and Rochdale

After 10 years away, York City are back in the EFL!

But it has not been all smooth sailing since. A couple of weeks before the start of the season, manager Stuart Maynard - who led them to promotion with more than 100 points - departed the club.

His replacement Scott Lindsey has not proven popular so far. In his first game in charge York exited the Carabao Cup at the preliminary phase, with fans booing and calling for the return of Maynard.

Not quite the return the Minstermen would have wanted to League Two.

The side they edged to automatic promotion in the National League, Rochdale, have also lost their manager after fighting their way through the play-offs.

McNulty moved on to Stockport, and they have dipped into non-League to appoint their new manager, with Ian Watson joining from National League North side South Shields.

Will Salford City finally get over the line?

Image: Macaulay Langstaff is one of the summer arrivals at Salford City

It is seven years now since Salford City were promoted to League Two, and still they have not managed to get over the line.

Last season was the closest they have come, losing in the play-off final to Notts County. Manager Karl Robinson has since departed, with Peter Cklamovski taking his place, having most recently been in charge of the Malaysia national side.

They have gone big in the transfer market, too. Macaulay Langstaff and Luke Molyneux have already arrived. Could this be the year the club owned by Gary Neville and David Beckham finally reach League One?

Managerial changes in League Two

Elsewhere, there are a lot of new managers to keep an eye on. Chris Hogg has come in at Northampton Town, while another relegated club in Rotherham United have appointed Alex Bruce.

Darrell Clarke takes charge at Tranmere Rovers, Lee Grant is at Walsall and Hayden Mullins will lead Newport County this season.

Sports.title: Sky Sports agrees deal to show Laver Cup from London's O2 in September
Sports.content:
Sky Sports has agreed a deal with Trident8 to show all three days of the Laver Cup from London's O2 arena this September, as 12 of the world's best men's players compete in the annual Europe vs 'Rest of the World' showdown.

World No 2 Carlos Alcaraz and Wimbledon finalist Alexander Zverev will be in action for Team Europe, while USA pair Ben Shelton and Taylor Fritz will lead the charge for Team World under the stewardship of captain Andre Agassi.

Hosted by presenter Gigi Salmon, Sky Sports will broadcast all 12 matches across day and night sessions on Friday September 25 and Saturday September 26, followed by a single concluding session on Sunday September 27. There will also be a reporter on the ground keeping fans abreast of all the news from the weekend's action.

Alongside broadcast rights, fans in the UK and Ireland will also be able to catch up on all the action with clips and highlights available across Sky's digital and social platforms.

Team Europe vice-captain and Sky Sports Tennis expert Tim Henman said: "It's great news the Laver Cup will be on Sky Sports.

"It's a unique opportunity to see the best players in the world coming together to represent Team Europe and Team World at the iconic O2 arena.

"Fans can expect plenty of drama, passion and rivalry, both on and off the court."

Live tennis is available all year on Sky Sports, including the Cincinnati Open beginning on Thursday August 13 and the US Open from Sunday August 30.

Sky Sports will broadcast over 4,000 matches and 80 tournaments this season, which are also available to stream with NOW and the Sky Sports app.

Watch the ATP and WTA Tours and US Open from August 30, live on Sky Sports or stream with NOW and the Sky Sports app

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 6: Chelsea
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 3rd (NB: this is not necessarily Billy Munday’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 10th

Prospects

After a season of struggle and regression, with two head coaches and two spells under a caretaker, there is cautious optimism that this campaign will bring something like stability. Much of that optimism centres around the appointment of Xabi Alonso, an elite manager with something to prove. There is also an expectation that the young players brought in as part of BlueCo’s £1.8bn splurge in recent years are beginning to come into their best years. There is no European football to complicate the schedule and a return to the Champions League by finishing in the top four or five would suffice for now. More importance will be placed on the domestic cups after a season without trophies.

Alonso’s squad is more rounded than what Enzo Maresca or Liam Rosenior had at their disposal. Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers bring quality to positions where Chelsea were lacking it – at centre-back and out wide. Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson – the “uncs” as Tosin Adarabioyo has called them – will contribute as much off the pitch as on it. The signing of Marco Palestra, a specialist wing-back, suggests Alonso wants to be tactically flexible. He has used a back four and a back three in pre-season.

What about Cole Palmer? For so much of his time at Stamford Bridge, Chelsea’s form has been tied to his. When he has struggled to be 100% fit, the team have suffered too. After being omitted from England’s World Cup squad, Palmer had a seven-week break and sought advice from a specialist on the groin injury that hampered him last season. “I got bored after six weeks,” Palmer said after returning for pre-season. “I was sat in Marbella thinking: ‘I want to go back in.’” With the prospect of linking up with Rogers and João Pedro, who has also had a good rest, Palmer has plenty of reasons to be excited.

Off-field picture

July ended with Chelsea being fined £10m and receiving a suspended transfer ban over multiple violations of transfer rules under the ownership of Roman Abramovich. An appeal from the club saved them from a six-point deduction. Chelsea were deemed compliant with the Premier League’s profitability and sustainability rules for the three-year period ending in 2025 despite posting an English record £262.4m pre-tax loss for the 2024-25 season. They have not been cowed by failure to qualify for Europe and have spent over £300m on new signings. For the fourth year in a row, Chelsea look likely to start the season without a front-of-shirt sponsor.

Owner-fan relationship

Supporter protests against the ownership of Todd Boehly’s BlueCo have been a frequent sight on matchdays, including before May’s FA Cup final defeat by Manchester City. There have been reservations about the club’s youth-oriented transfer policy from the start and last season’s failings prompted the co-owner Behdad Eghbali to admit the need “to add more ready-made players” to the squad. Whether fans were expecting the arrivals of Welbeck and Henderson is another question. The introduction of a ticket ballot system for home games has also been unpopular with regular match-going supporters.

The manager

It was a bit of a coup for Chelsea to secure Alonso’s services this summer, especially given the Liverpool job was available. The Spaniard has a reputation to rebuild after his dream job at Real Madrid ended in the sack after six months. “I got a scar, now it is healed,” he said. Alonso’s record of developing young players, such as Florian Wirtz, at Bayer Leverkusen while simultaneously delivering silverware is a match made in heaven for the Chelsea hierarchy. One detail to note: Alonso has been appointed as manager, rather than head coach like his predecessors. He has also brought in Austin MacPhee, Aston Villa’s set-piece guru.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Chelsea broke the British transfer record to pry Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Chelsea went one better than Manchester City’s £116m signing of Elliot Anderson by bringing in Rogers, who had been linked with Arsenal, for a new British record fee of £117m. Although he started England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina on the right wing, Rogers has thrived for Aston Villa playing largely off the left and should slot in there nicely at Chelsea. The 24-year-old has proved himself in the Premier League and his best-buddy relationship with his former Manchester City youth teammate Palmer is a major plus. “I can see them linking really well,” Alonso said.

Stat attack

Has anyone checked Chelsea haven’t built a squad of Benjamin Buttons? The average age of their starting XI has decreased over the past three seasons when they were already the youngest team in Premier League history. You can see why they signed Henderson and Welbeck.

Set for a breakthrough

Robert Sánchez is still Chelsea’s No 1 but he may face serious competition this season from the 21-year-old Mike Penders. The goalkeeper, who was third-choice for Belgium at the World Cup, was signed from Genk in 2024 and spent last season on loan at Strasbourg in Ligue 1. The comparisons with Thibaut Courtois, who Chelsea signed from Genk at a similar age, are obvious. Like Courtois, Penders is 6ft 7in and therefore has a massive reach, but he also earns plaudits for his passing. Chances will come in cup competitions, but the clamour for Penders to be first choice might become hard to ignore.

World Cup impact

Enzo Fernández had a rollercoaster of a World Cup. Chelsea’s vice-captain popped up with crucial late goals for Argentina in the knockout stages, including a winning header against Egypt and the equaliser against England. But the abiding memory was his part in Argentina’s unsavoury approach in the final against Spain, where he received one yellow card for dissent and another for sending Pau Cubarsí flying. Real Madrid said in July they had “no intention” of pursuing a move that Fernández seemed to covet earlier this year when he said he would “love” to live in Madrid – comments that earned him a two-game ban under Rosenior. How about living in Manchester? City have been linked.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi has ‘quite a few doubts’ about football future after death of his father
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi said on Wednesday that he is having doubts about continuing his career following the death of his father last week. Messi’s father, ⁠Jorge, died last week aged 68 at a medical clinic in the Argentinian city of Rosario after a long illness.

In a tribute on Instagram, Messi wrote: “I don’t know what I’m going to ⁠do without you. I ⁠don’t know how ​to move forward. I only played football and now I have quite a few doubts about whether I’m going to keep doing it for much ⁠longer.

“You were by my side from the beginning; there was so little left until the end. Why couldn’t you hold on just ⁠a little longer so we could finish it together?”

Jorge closely accompanied his son throughout his career, beginning ​with his early years at Barcelona. He acted ‌as a crucial pillar of ‌support and, for several years, served as his representative.

The 39-year-old Argentina captain revealed one of the reasons he ‌played in the World Cup, where they finished runners-up to Spain after an extra-time defeat in the final, was because it was his father’s wish.

“You always asked me to play in the last World Cup and a few days before it started was when you got worse,” Messi said. “It was the first time you weren’t going to be at a tournament … Every time a match ended, I would ‌wait and hope for your message. That’s when I realised how real the situation was.”

During the World Cup, Messi experienced mixed emotions after scoring a hat-trick in ​the opening match against Algeria, breaking down in tears while celebrating his first goal. He later explained that his tears were due to “something unrelated to football” after going through “a few difficult, complicated days”.

Messi said he wanted to win the final for his father but he had no energy left to bring home a second World Cup title. “My ⁠legs couldn’t go on any more. This time I tried to push myself beyond my ​physical limits, but I couldn’t. ​I never felt well … We weren’t champions, ​but you don’t know how much we enjoyed every match. Once again, you were ​right: I had to ‌be there and play ​it.”

Despite his ​grief, the Inter Miami forward pledged to honour his father’s memory through parenting his own children. “I’m going to miss you so much, but you will always be present, especially in the upbringing of my children, because I will teach them and raise them the way you raised me.”

Sports.title: ‘It’s a nice hobby’: Manchester United’s Janina Leitzig on goalkeeping and gardening
Sports.content:
With some parts of England gearing up for a fifth heatwave of 2026 the new Manchester United goalkeeper Janina Leitzig, a keen gardener, is sympathetic to the precarious health of this reporter’s tomato plants. “You’re not used to so little rain, are you?” she observes. For the time being, after her summer move to Manchester, the former Germany youth international does not have a garden of her own but she reveals that, during her three-and-a-half-year spell at her former club Leicester, homegrown vegetables were her pride and joy.

“I love to do some gardening. Back home, everyone has their own vegetables and it’s just better, it tastes better,” she tells the Guardian. “Being away from home and away from family, of course you have your football friends, but still it can be quite lonely sometimes if you come home from training, so it was really nice to have a garden and to spend time outside. It’s not too much effort, it’s just a nice hobby.”

The 27-year-old got her outdoor fix with a spot of surfing in Cornwall this summer during the off-season, but now the serious business of pre-season is well under way. Her new club Manchester United are heading to La Manga for a training camp between 14 and 19 August, where the focus will have to be less on runner beans and more on running drills.

Leitzig, the former Bayern Munich and Hoffenheim keeper, was sitting down for an interview before it was known that the Spanish coach Eva Olid was to become United’s new manager, but explained why swapping Leicester for United was appealing to her. “It’s such a big club and it’s such a big honour to be here,” Leitzig says.

“I think, for every player, it’s really interesting if you have an offer from Manchester United. First of all, the team is so nice. The characters in here – you can tell it’s a really good and strong team. The training quality is really high. The building and the facilities [at Carrington] are really good; it’s really professional here. [When] the conversations were going on [with United], they just gave me a really good feeling.”

View image in fullscreen Janina Leitzig during a training session at Carrington. Photograph: Poppy Townson/MUFC/Getty Images

Leitzig has signed a contract with United until 2029, after the disappointment of relegation with Leicester last season, but says she has nothing but fond feelings about her former club, who she initially joined on loan in January 2023 before signing permanently that summer.

Looking back at what she learned in the East Midlands, she says: “It was such a special time for me. It was supposed to be only half a year and then it ended up being three-and-a-half. I think that says a lot about how much I liked it there. The people are great and the club is great.

“Obviously we had some tough times and unfortunately the relegation last season was really, really tough and it really hurt, because the club deserves to be in a better position, but I really hope that the girls will do well and I see them soon back in the WSL. It would be great if they could come back up quickly.”

During her time in England, Leitzig has observed an evolution in goalkeeping styles, and she is in a thoughtful mood when discussing what the future might look like for keepers, tactically. On the modern trend of keepers playing out from the back, she says: “To be fair, there was one phase where everyone wanted goalkeepers to play with the feet and I think it’s still really important, but I think there was a phase where it was too much. I think it was a bit overexaggerated at times, so I think it’s coming back now to be more about the basic stuff.

“Obviously you have to switch play and you have to be good with your feet under pressure, but I think the game is going to be more [about] trying to get the ball as quick as possible in the opposite half to then keep the pressure up there and not to try to take such a high risk. It’s going to be interesting.

“I think, because I’m German and Manuel Neuer [her idol] is German, I learned quite early to play with both feet and I was an outfield player initially, so I’m feeling confident about playing with the ball. But saving shots is the best part of goalkeeping.”

The USA keeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce played in 21 of United’s 22 matches in the Women’s Super League last season and Leitzig says they will enjoy working together and helping each other. “They [United] said it’s like a competition [to start in goal]. Obviously it’s really important to have strong goalkeepers, because you never know what happens in the season.

“I will just give my best, I’ll try to bring quality, and then it’s the manager’s decision to decide who’s going to play. But it’s really important that we are a good goalkeeper team, that we support each other and push each other because then everyone can get better.”

United, who finished fourth last season, will get the new WSL season under way on the opening night, at London City Lionesses on 4 September. Leizig concludes by looking ahead to that showdown and says, with fire in her eyes: “To have the first game of the season Friday evening, 7pm, floodlights, it’s just something you’re really excited for. Working in the pre-season you think: ‘When can the [games] finally start,’ so I’m really excited for that game.”

Sports.title: Barcelona make improved £51m bid for Rodri as Manchester City target Fernández
Sports.content:
Barcelona have made an improved bid to Manchester City of around €60m (£51m) for Rodri. This follows Barça’s initial offer of €45m that was rejected out of hand by City.

The Spanish club’s new offer – which may include add-ons – is close to City’s valuation for the 30-year-old who captained Spain to the World Cup and won the Ballon d’Or in 2024.

As the midfielder has declared a preference for Barcelona it seems it is inevitable he will leave. In preparation City are targeting Chelsea’s Enzo Fernández as a potential signing though the west London club’s valuation of around £120m may be too high.

Chelsea are understood to be intent on that price for the attacking midfielder so any transfer may include add-ons. Enzo Maresca is keen on Fernández after working with him for a season-and-a-half at Chelsea before his tenure ended in January.

The 25-year-old was a key member of Maresca’s team that finished fourth and won the Europa Conference in 2024-25 and the Fifa Club World Cup last summer.

If City were to sign Fernández, a World Cup winner with Argentina in 2022, another midfielder could be offloaded, with Tijjani Reijnders a possible candidate to depart.

As Rodri is intent on a move to Barcelona the arrival of Fernández, Chelsea’s captain, would add seniority and leadership to Maresca’s squad and a player whose combative style would offer an edge to City’s play.

City have so far recruited Elliott Anderson for £116m from Nottingham Forest and are close to the signing of Ayyoub Bouaddi for around £85m from Lille.

Chelsea are thought to have enquired about Bournemouth’s Alex Scott as a replacement for Fernández should he leave.

The 34-year-old said: “My job now is to train hard, get to know the players and staff and do everything I can.”

Sports.title: Championship angst: why the sense of rejuvenation in EFL is not universal
Sports.content:
A new season is supposed to be about renewed hope and optimism, a fresh campaign opening up a world of possibilities, a clean slate. But with the English Football League due to kick off on Friday night when Wolves host Blackburn in the Championship, the sense of rejuvenation is not universal.

The lineup of Championship teams this season is fearsome. Wolves and West Ham, hitherto established Premier League clubs, have dropped into the second tier. Others such as Burnley, Middlesbrough and Southampton anticipate a promotion push. So perhaps supporters of those who are not enjoying parachute payment riches and squads still packed with top-flight talent are wise to feel cautious. Some fear a long slog of a season to come.

Blackburn fans, for example, saw their side scrape to the safety of a 20th-place finish last season, therefore would be forgiven for tempering their expectations before the trip to Molineux. Tony Mowbray has been brought back to Ewood Park as an experienced guiding hand, but the 62-year-old has a huge task to avoid a relegation battle.

Fans believe the Rovers owners and the club’s head of football operations, Rudy Gestede, have sold Mowbray short on players heading into the season, particularly in midfield. The 34-year-old Sam Morsy – described by Mowbray as “a real man, a soldier” – has added steel to that area of the pitch with his free transfer, but after Moussa Baradji and Jayden Fevrier he is only the third addition at Blackburn this summer. Mowbray wants and needs more.

“I’m a bit greedy for good players,” he said. “I keep saying to Rudy: ‘I just want good players, doesn’t really matter where they come from, what age they are.’ I want to see personality on the pitch, players who are desperate to win.”

Blackburn edged past Burton 2-1 in the Carabao Cup first round last week, though they required late goals from Andri Gudjohnsen and Fevrier, who Mowbray believes can bring “magic” on the right wing after signing from Stockport.

View image in fullscreen Bolton Wanderers celebrated victory in the League One playoff final but a tricky season lies ahead. Photograph: Nigel French/PA

Down the road, there are two other Championship clubs feeling a similar sense of trepidation before the new campaign, and they meet at the Toughsheet Stadium on Saturday lunchtime, a game that could set the tone for their seasons. Bolton should still be on cloud nine; they finished last season with a 4-1 demolition of Stockport in the League One playoff final. Yet as the football world has witnessed this summer at York – where the manager, Stuart Maynard, was sacked and replaced by Scott Lindsey, despite winning the National League with 108 points – the afterglow of promotion can be short-lived. Reality bites quick.

And such is the chasm between the second and third tiers nowadays, the need for Steven Schumacher’s side to strengthen fast became paramount after that glorious day at Wembley. David Watson, Ben Davies, Akin Famewo, Luca Stephenson, Kyliane Dong and Gaizka Larrazabal have all arrived, but there is a feeling among the fanbase that a marquee addition is needed, especially in attack where they risk asking too much of the striker Sam Dalby. Schumacher’s admission last week that Bolton “can’t afford to waste money” rang alarm bells with the fanbase. There is not an embarrassment of riches in the pot but forward players must be signed.

“We know we’re short, especially at the top end of the pitch,” Schumacher said. “Our budget isn’t massive so we need to make sure we get the right players in, rather than just signing anybody to fill numbers. We need to try and consolidate this year, rebuild, get some more finances behind us, bring in a better squad that can keep us at this level, and then kick on.”

Schumacher said that “this part of the journey is an exciting one” but it seems negativity among some fans has kicked in before a Championship ball has been kicked. A 1-0 defeat against Sheffield Wednesday in the Carabao Cup reinforced concerns around goalscoring, or the lack of it. Max Dean of Gent is coveted, but the striker is just 22 and his English football experience is limited to a short spell at MK Dons.

Preston will hope to take advantage of the uncertainty around Bolton on Saturday, but Paul Heckingbottom has endured his own problems in the transfer market this summer. A public spat with Ben Whiteman over the midfielder’s desire to join Wrexham left a cloud hanging above the club and saw the Lilywhites lose their club captain. Heckingbottom said Whiteman “crossed a line” and was frustrated by the saga.

Money has been spent at Deepdale this summer with Alfie Devine brought in from Tottenham for a fee in the region of £6m, while Callum Lang “feels like a new signing” according to Heckingbottom, having arrived in January for around £2m before getting injured. So the pressure is on Heckingbottom perhaps like never before. A run of just four wins from their final 20 matches of last season prompted a few fan murmurs of discontent towards the manager. With Preston almost investing £1.5m to install a modern hybrid pitch at Deepdale, the club expect better than last season’s 14th-place finish, but expectations can weigh heavy.

Sports.title: ‘It is just smelling football’: Tielemans says adjusting to life at United has come naturally
Sports.content:
Youri Tielemans has stated that adjusting to Michael Carrick’s vision for Manchester United has been as easy as “smelling football” for the vastly experienced £35m midfield signing.

The 29-year-old, who joined from Aston Villa last month, made his debut for Anderlecht at the age of 16. He has been integrating with the United squad during the past 10 days of the club’s pre-season tour, making his first appearance in the 1-1 draw with Paris Saint-Germain in Gothenburg on Saturday.

Tielemans left Belgium for Monaco in 2017 and joined Leicester in 2019, before signing for Villa four years later and has 579 career appearances, so any demands from Carrick do not faze him.

Tielemans said: “He has got his structure. He wants to have the ball, he wants to press in certain ways, you know. It might be different than what you are used to, what I have been used to before, but it is logical things in my opinion. It is just smelling football, and that is what I have been doing from when I was young at Anderlecht.

“So for me, nothing changes, but it just needs to gel together. Then when you follow those principles, then you can add your offensive qualities, especially in the last third where everything is a bit more in freedom, without obviously overcommitting and keeping the defensive line in place, then I think we can do good things.”

Tielemans was limited to only 25 starts in the Premier League last season because of injury and also sustained a hamstring problem in the warm-up before Belgium’s World Cup quarter-final against Spain in July. Yet despite this and having already played for 13 years in midfield, Tielemans denied that Carrick will need to rest him on occasion.

He said: “Not really. The thing is, at the World Cup, I think we played 120 minutes against Senegal [before Spain], and from there we had less time in between games. So we played the US I think three or four days later [actually five days] and then three days later we played against Spain. In the warm-up, my body just switched off for some reason. Now, I do not think I am a player that I absolutely need a rest. Obviously, there are a lot of games and the manager needs to manage the team, but when I am good I am good, you know.

“Unfortunately, my body is … when it does not go well, then I will know straight away and I will alert the manager, but it does not happen often.”

United previously showed interest in signing the Belgium captain, reportedly in 2019 and 2022. “There has been two times that I spoke with the club, but it did not achieve to anything, so I was just very calm about it. It was way after Anderlecht,” Tielemans said.

United, who triggered his release clause, did not face any competition to sign the player. “Not that I am aware of, no,” Tielemans said.

Sports.title: Saudi Pro League tries to move on from era of ageing megastar but big names still loom | John Duerden
Sports.content:
There is no Mohamed Salah in the new Saudi Pro League season that kicks off on Thursday and while the era of the ageing megastar is ending, there is still the strong chance that the next few months will be dominated by Cristiano Ronaldo. The 41-year-old is 24 shy of 1,000 career goals and, with the five-time Ballon d’Or winner having scored 102 in 107 league games for Al-Nassr so far, the milestone could – should – be reached this season.

Huge as that will be, just how it fits into the plans of the league is unclear. This is the fourth season since the spending started with $957m (£710m) splashed out in that summer of 2023. It delivered thousands of articles, dozens of international broadcasting deals and untold numbers of people worldwide sporting the yellow CR7 Al-Nassr shirt. Now, though, the focus is on getting a little more value for money and lifting not just the clubs but the standard of Saudi Arabian football in general.

An early World Cup elimination provoked plenty of questions (even if later results showed that draws against Uruguay and an impressive Cape Verde plus a sole defeat against the champions Spain wasn’t quite as bad as it first looked) with the main one being whether the money spent on the local league had resulted in a better standard of local players. As yet, it does not seem to be the case.

The league does not yet supply talent to Europe, or anywhere else. Of the 26-man World Cup squad only the right-back Saud Abdulhamid of Lens plays overseas. The consensus is that this has to change, and is heightened by the worry that too many of those who stay home don’t get enough minutes. Locals are often squeezed out by foreign talents, especially when it comes to creative, goalscoring and goalkeeping positions. The big spending has undoubtedly improved the standard of teams in general – Saudi sides have had increased success in Asian club competitions – but the national side has yet to see the benefit.

So while many expected Salah to choose the Red Sea over the Black Sea port of Trabzonspor, the determination to get the Egyptian seemed to have lessened over the past few months (and that’s assuming that Salah ever considered Saudi Arabia as his first choice). The biggest name in the Arab footballing world would have been quite a draw even if the 34-year-old no longer fits the preferred model, which is trying to sign younger players who have a resale value when they return to Europe.

It remains to be seen if that is the case for Crysencio Summerville, the biggest signing of the summer so far, who joined Al-Hilal for around €80m (£68m). If all goes well, the 24-year old Dutch winger can spend some time in Riyadh and, one day, head back to Europe for another hefty fee. There have been the usual criticisms of Summerville choosing money over ambition but ambition is part of the Hilal DNA. With 19 league titles and four Asian championships, coming second again will not be acceptable even if the team were undefeated through the whole campaign. The Blues, sold by the Public Investment Fund in April, still have Karim Benzema, Rúben Neves, Theo Hernández, Yassine Bounou, Kalidou Koulibaly and more, so the pressure is on the head coach, Simone Inzaghi, to retake the title from the yellow half of Riyadh.

View image in fullscreen Saud Abdulhamid is the only player from Saudi Arabia to play overseas, with Lens. Photograph: Icon Sport/Alamy

Ronaldo lifted that trophy in May for Al-Nassr, a triumph soon followed by the exit of Jorge Jesus to take over Portugal. He has been replaced by Ange Postecoglou. The former Tottenham manager has Sadio Mané, Kingsley Coman and João Félix at his disposal, but the club have financial issues which have meant that, as yet, there have not been many incomings. A first Asian Champions League title would go down well.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That crown belongs to Al-Ahli who, after winning their second successive continental title in April, were ready to focus on domestic matters this season and a second SPL title since 1984. It was all looking good but then, just a few days before the start, the head coach Matthias Jaissle left for Newcastle. The Greens and the Magpies may share the same PIF owner but this was not a decision that went down well in Jeddah. The appointment of Arne Slot’s former assistant Marino Pusic is not seen as especially exciting. Jaissle’s departure also came as a shock to Jeddah rivals Al-Ittihad, who struggled last season. Just a day or so before Jaissle’s departure, the Tigers followed their rivals in hiring a 38-year-old German, whose career as a defender had also been cut short by injury and had experience at RB Salzburg. Jens Wissing has a big job ahead.

And Al-Qadsiah are the last of the contenders. If Brendan Rodgers can improve on the fourth-place finish of last season and also win a first trophy since 1984, that will be enough for the Aramco-backed club. There is now a genuine “big five” which provides challenges for the others but perhaps they can progress by giving more minutes and opportunities to local players which would, in the long run, be better for the league than signing Salah and other players in their mid-30s.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Folarin Balogun to Tottenham? Gabriel Jesus to Napoli?
Sports.content:
Bradley Barcola is firmly in Liverpool’s sights as they look to rebuild their attack in the post-Mohamed Salah era. The two-time Champions League winner reportedly wants to leave Paris Saint-Germain, and Anfield is his preferred destination, though Arsenal have apparently been making eyes at the France international too. For their part PSG are thought to be closing on deals for Barcelona’s World Cup winner Ferran Torres and the Ajax winger Mika Godts, though the 21-year-old Belgium international had talked at the weekend of “putting an end” to rumours that he was refusing to play for Ajax in order to force a move.

England’s World Cup cult hero Djed Spence could soon be exhibiting his marauding runs and eye-catching slide tackles in Serie A. Inter are interested in a £25.6m move for the Tottenham full-back, who fancies a move to San Siro and might find himself struggling for regular first-team football in north London after Roberto De Zerbi’s busy summer in the market.

Napoli are stepping up their interest in Gabriel Jesus, who could be available for around €20m (£17m). With the Arsenal striker entering the final year of his contract at the Emirates and first-team opportunities with the English champions likely to be limited, Jesus could be amenable to a move. Arsenal meanwhile are keen on Jules Koundé, reports the Mirror, but an awful lot of ifs and ands are in play around the Barcelona and France full-back. For one Koundé is happy to stay at the Camp Nou, even if Barça might be prepared to cash in on a player with four years remaining on his contract, and the Spanish champions’ preferred replacement, Pedro Porro, has five years to go on his after recently signing a new deal with Tottenham.

As for Spurs, a rumoured target is controversy’s Folarin Balogun. L’Equipe says talks have been initiated with Monaco about a €60m (£51.2m) move for the USA and former Arsenal striker, who impressed at the World Cup. Another Monaco player attracting Premier League interest is the winger Igor Paixao, at whom Leeds continue to make eyes. The Ligue 1 club’s manager, Bruno Genesio, is eager to keep the Brazilian though.

Mykhailo Mudryk could be sent to Coventry on his return from drug-ban limbo. Chelsea are open to loan offers for the Ukrainian winger and Frank Lampard’s newly promoted side have jostled their way to the front of the queue, according to football.london.

Everton are weighing up their interest in three full-backs – Celtic’s Alastair Johnson, West Ham’s Aaron Wan-Bissaka and the English right-back Brooke Norton-Cuffy, who has been at Genoa since 2024. David Moyes will also be cheered by news that Iliman Ndiaye has reportedly turned down a move to the Saudi Pro League’s Al-Hilal. Fulham meanwhile like the look of the 20-year-old Barcelona defender Hector Fort, who spent last season on loan at Elche and does not appear to have a future at the Camp Nou.

And Wednesday’s Manchester United rumour has the Red Devils in for the Club Brugge left-back Joaquin Seys. The 21-year-old Belgium international would set them back around £30m.

Sports.title: Rory Jennings unveils five-point plan to save football and oust Gianni Infantino including instant relegation for ‘game’s gone’ offence
Sports.content:
Rory Jennings has revealed how he would revamp football if he were FIFA president.

Current FIFA boss Gianni Infantino remains under fire amid the fallout from his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, with UEFA maintaining its threat to boycott future World Cups.

2 Infantino is up for re-election next year but is losing the support of FIFA member associations Credit: AFP

US president Donald Trump has said it would be a 'terrible mistake' if Infantino were to be replaced (having last month backed him to head up the United Nations), but the 56-year-old is losing the support of FIFA member nations.

And on Tuesday's talkSPORT DriveTime, Jamie O'Hara put Jennings forward for the role of FIFA president.

So, in a world with Jennings in charge of the game, what would change?

Well, there are five things...

"Right, the first thing that I do," Jennings began, "there is a cap on ticket prices. It is now impossible for dynamic pricing to exist.

"And I'm going to be completely fair: if it's a World Cup final, for example, an FA Cup final, a Champions League final... Tickets cannot cost more than £1,000. That is the max.

"And I appreciate that's incredibly expensive and probably still too dear, but I'm trying to do this as fairly as possible and almost as realistically as possible."

But there's more, as Jennings explained: "A percentage of tickets goes to local fans for a token amount.

"So, regardless of the club, anywhere in the world, a percentage of tickets has to be available for a peppercorn amount of money to local fans. If you live within a 10-mile radius of the stadium, a percentage of tickets will be allocated to you for a maximum of £30 a ticket."

And Jennings has another idea to improve the atmosphere in grounds.

"You increase away tickets in every stadium to 15 per cent," he continued. "Atmospheres in this country are really struggling. Football stadiums have become so sanitised, so boring, so corporate that you need to elevate the atmosphere.

2 Jennings wants more fans to be able to support their team away from home Credit: AFP

"The way that you do it is by giving away more tickets to the away fans. Not every club can do it, but they will have the option of taking 15 per cent of the stadium."

On top of that, there's one thing Jennings is desperate to see the back of at games – or clubs will face severe consequences, much to the amusement of O'Hara.

"You ban, you immediately ban music after a goal that's scored," he insisted. "Any club that plays a song after a goal is scored are relegated straight away.

"If you play a song – so, Chelsea are doing it now – it's so not who we are; it's so against our culture."

Nor does Jennings have any time for 'stattos' in football...

"We're banning all statto types," he went on. "Anyone that bases their footballing opinions not from playing the game, not from going to the game [but] from stats, from computers.

"If you want to talk about anything like that...talk about progressive passes, talk about pie charts, talk about anything like that... That is all immediately banned as is...You can use stats to enhance your opinion, but you can't form your opinion off stats."

Sports.title: Paris Saint-Germain granted last-minute request before Aston Villa Super Cup clash after complaining to UEFA
Sports.content:
Paris Saint-Germain have been given an extra dressing room for Wednesday's Super Cup encounter with Aston Villa.

The European champions had complained to UEFA after Villa were allocated the home dressing room at the Red Bull Arena in Salzburg, Austria, leaving them using the smaller away facilities.



2 Red Bull Salzburg's Red Bull Arena plays host to the 2026 UEFA Super Cup Credit: Getty

PSG were said to be unhappy about not being given the same amount of changing space as Villa.

And UEFA have responded by allowing Luis Enrique's side to also use the dressing room normally reserved for the match officials. It's not clear where the officials, with Somali referee Omar Artan in charge of the game, will get changed.

PSG have travelled to Austria with a squad of 20 players, including new signing Lucas Digne – who joined from Villa earlier this week.



Having retained their Champions League crown last season, Les Parisiens are looking to do likewise with the Super Cup.

They beat Tottenham on penalties in Udine, Italy last year to lift the trophy for the first time.



Luis Enrique admits his team's preparations this time around have been less than ideal, though, largely due to players returning from World Cup duty at different points of the summer.

"We suffered many absences during the pre-season matches, and therefore it is difficult to predict who will be able to play," he said at his pre-match press conference on Tuesday.



"I do not have players. Some players returned on Monday, and others returned last week. We are trying to prepare in the best possible way, but I do not know what physical condition our players will be in."

This will be the 51st edition of the Super Cup, played annually between the winners of the previous season's Champions League and Europa League since 2000 (until 1999, it was played between the winners of the Champions League and Cup Winners' Cup).

Villa emphatically beat Freiburg 3-0 in May's final to claim their first major trophy for 30 years.

2 Unai Emery is eyeing his second trophy as Villa boss Credit: Getty



In doing so, manager Unai Emery sealed a record-extending fifth Europa League triumph.

Villa previously won the Super Cup in 1982 as European champions, defeating Barcelona 3-1 over two legs.

Looking ahead to his side's first competitive outing of the 2026/27 campaign, Emery highlighted the chance to win more silverware.

"Of course, it's an opportunity," he told reporters. A trophy is something that can give us a special moment. To play for trophies is, as a professional, our objective.



"PSG are the favourites but I am looking forward to playing, how we can test this match against PSG with our capacity?

"As a coach, as a player, as a club, it's a trophy. It's one thing that makes us proud of how we are and how we arrive here."

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo sends classy message to Lionel Messi as icon posts emotional message after father’s death
Sports.content:
“Dad, I still can’t believe that you’ve gone. It hasn’t sunk in, or better said, I won’t let it sink in.

“It’s so hard to imagine that now I’m not going to see you anymore, that we’re not going to talk anymore. I know you were suffering and that this is for the best, but you went so soon. We still had so much left to enjoy together

“You kept asking me to play in this last World Cup but just days before it started, your condition took a turn for the worse. It was the first time you wouldn’t be at a tournament, but Mum told me that you were going to get better and you’d be able to travel.

“Each time I finished a game, I’d wait for and miss your message. That’s when I realized the situation was truly dire. Even so, I kept thinking about going as far as possible to buy time so you could watch a game. We made it to the final, but you couldn’t be there. I wanted to win it so I could bring it to you and show you a new trophy. I couldn’t do it; my legs just gave out. This time I tried to push past my physical limits, but I couldn’t. I just never felt right.”

“When I got to you, you thought we had lost the final on penalties. We couldn’t talk about any of what had happened. You weren't able to enjoy anything. We didn’t become champions, but you didn’t know how much we enjoyed each game. Once again you were right - I had to be there and play.

“I’m telling you this because it was the one thing we couldn't talk about; you already know everything else. We spoke every day and saw each other whenever my commitments allowed.

“I don’t know what I’m going to do without you, I don’t know how to carry on. All I’ve ever done is play football and now I have so many doubts over whether I’m going to keep doing it for much longer. You were by my side from the start, and we were so close to the end. Why couldn't you hold on just a little longer so we could finish it together?

“I know your happiness was in seeing your family doing well, your wife, your kids, and above all, without letting the others know, watching me play.

“Since I was a young boy it was always this way. You took me to every training session, right after getting home from work. Mum took me to many of them because you were working.

“Obviously you never missed a single match. How you suffered while watching me, and how you enjoyed it—even though you never lavished me with praise.

“You were my dad, my friend and my representative. You were always exactly who you needed to be in any given moment, and you never got it wrong. Beyond the odd argument or disagreement, you were always right; in the end, things always turned out just as you said they would.

“I’m going to miss you so much, but you will always be present, and above all in how I raise my kids, because I’ll raise them and teach them the way you did with me.

“Rest in peace and look after us from above just as you did down here. Thank you for everything.

“I love you, Dad.”

Sports.title: Championship club granted permission to build ‘vomitory’ at stadium
Sports.content:
Burnley have been granted permission to build a 'vomitory' at Turf Moor by the local council.

The Clarets, who are back in the Championship this season, will now create a new access point in the Barnfield Stand.

2 Changes will soon be made to Turf Moor - which will host Championship football this season Credit: Getty

Despite suggesting that it has something to do with sick that isn't the case at all.

A vomitory is simply a large passageway or staircase designed to help large crowds enter and leave a venue quickly.

The origins of the word are Latin and descend from 'vomere', which means to spew forth.

The plan is for this to be a staircase making the upper part of the stand easier to access.

It will also serve as a fire escape and is expected to be all weather.

Plans detail that the structure will be covered in black metal cladding, with the inside containing Burnley's crest.

However, construction of the 'vomitory' could be delayed due to the possibility of coal beneath the ground.

Burnley Council have approved the plans but on the condition that the Coal Mining Authority inspect before anything is constructed due to concerns over stability.

In a statement, the Coal Mining Authority said: “While the proposed development is a relatively lightweight structure any increased loading could induce further instability of the workings.”

They added that an inspection would need to be conducted: “This investigation should comprise a series of at least three boreholes advanced approximately 15m into solid bedrock.”

2 Kyle Walker will hope to lead Burnley back to the Premier League Credit: Getty

Other changes

The addition of a 'vomitory' isn't the only change happening at Turf Moor.

The club are planning to install some LED signage outside of the ground on Harry Potts Way.

There are also controversial plans to allow the club to close roads around the ground on matchdays.

New season, high hopes

Meanwhile, on the pitch, Burnley are looking to bounce back from Premier League relegation last year with promotion.

Scott Parker is gone and he has been replaced by Nicky Hayen, who got off to a winning start at the weekend.

The EFL kicked off the season with the Carabao Cup first round, and Hayen's side were at home to Notts County.

They needed penalties, but they did see off the League One side, winning 4-3 in the shootout after a 1-1 draw.

After the game, Hayen felt his players weren't aggressive enough in their opener.

He said: “We want to have creativity in the final third. But not only creativity, we also need deep runs.

“It's something that we worked on last week and we still have to improve these kinds of things.

“Sometimes we want to make it too nice. We have the space, play the ball or bring the ball in front of the goal. Now, we want to play too nice and then suddenly you lose the ball and you have a transition moment that you sprint 70 metres back.

“So this is something that we have to increase. Let's say play more clinical and not only too fancy, but it will come by the weeks.”

Certainly, they'll have to be sharper for their opening Championship match this weekend.

They host West Ham, live on talkSPORT 2 on Sunday, August 16.

Kick-off at Turf Moor is scheduled for 4pm, and our live coverage is hosted by Max Scott.

Commentary comes from Adam Bridge and former Burnley striker Chris Iwelumo.

To tune in to talkSPORT through the website, click HERE for the live stream.

You can also listen via the talkSPORT app, on DAB digital radio, through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.
