World.title: Three-time Olympian Lolo Jones says Team USA 'abandoned' her after harrowing spinal injury
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Lolo Jones is not backing down after a harrowing experience with Team USA.

In February 2025, Jones climbed into a team-issued bobsled at the Olympic training complex in Lake Placid, New York. The U.S. team was testing equipment before the World Championships. The sled accelerated down the ice at speeds approaching 90 mph.

At the bottom of the track, Jones knew something was wrong.

Her lower back burned. She could not bend over. She had lost control of her bladder.

"I’ve never had that happen to me ever in (my) life," Jones said. "I immediately went up to the athletic trainer and told him what was happening."

Jones was no inexperienced athlete struggling to read her body. She competed at the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics as a hurdler and the 2014 Winter Olympics as a bobsled brakewoman. She had won world championships in both sports.

She understood pain. This felt different.

SIMONE BILES RETURNS TO HOSPITAL FOR PROCEDURE WEEKS AFTER 'ALMOST DYING' IN 'MEDICAL EMERGENCY'

A trainer arranged a treatment for her, but Jones says the head of sports medicine at the Lake Placid training center canceled it because she had already received treatment that week.

Jones arrived for the appointment without knowing it had been canceled.

She was hurt, frightened and days away from the biggest race of the season.

TENNESSEE COACH UNLOADS ON NCAA'S 'BULLS–T', AFTER STAR LINEBACKER SUSPENDED FOR OUTDATED RULE

Then Jones received notice that officials had revoked her access to sports medicine, she says, and a broader ban later kept her out of the Olympic training facility, including its rehabilitation areas, weight room, housing and push track.

The notice said her behavior violated the facility’s code of conduct, she says, but Jones claims officials never identified the specific rule she broke or gave her a formal hearing before imposing the punishment.

According to reporting by the Southern California News Group, Jones and other people familiar with the case said USOPC officials later acknowledged that the approved treatment should not have been canceled. Jones apologized during a meeting before the World Championships.

The restrictions remained.

SIMONE BILES FIRES BACK AT INSTAGRAM USERS WHO MOCKED HER NEAR-DEATH EXPERIENCE, REVEALS MEDICAL EMERGENCY

"I voiced my frustration that athletes should have medical access," Jones said. "It just continued to escalate."

The symptoms Jones described demanded more than a routine massage.

Severe back pain combined with bladder dysfunction can signal compression of the nerves at the base of the spinal cord.

The American Association of Neurological Surgeons lists urinary incontinence, leg weakness and severe lower-back pain among the warning signs of cauda equina syndrome, a medical emergency that can cause permanent paralysis or loss of bladder control.

Jones says no one at the center examined her, ordered imaging or explained the possible severity of her injury.

Without a diagnosis, she made the decision elite athletes often make. She kept going.

Jones obtained pain medication from her doctor in Louisiana and returned to the sled for the World Championships in Lake Placid. She completed four runs with pilot Elana Meyers Taylor. They finished sixth.

"If someone would’ve told me, ‘Your spinal fluid is leaking out of your back. If that pilot hits a wall, you will be paralyzed,’ there is no way I would’ve gotten back in that bobsled," Jones said.

After the championships, Jones paid for her own MRI. She says the imaging revealed a herniated disc, another disc bulge, several lumbar tears and a cerebrospinal-fluid leak. She later underwent spinal surgery.

She also paid for rehabilitation, travel and private medical help while she remained barred from the training center. She estimates the injury and its aftermath cost her about $100,000.

For Jones, the cost exposes a larger imbalance inside Olympic sports.

Many bobsled athletes survive on modest stipends while absorbing significant training and travel expenses. Jones had income from work outside the sport, but she says the bills still devastated her finances.

"I make good money, but I’m not making Michael Phelps money," she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Jones now argues that Olympic athletes need stronger due-process protections and an affordable way to challenge the institutions that control their medical care, funding and competitive futures. She says the current grievance system costs too much and gives athletes little realistic power against governing bodies.

The experience has also changed how she views the Olympics themselves.

Jones once imagined that a future daughter might follow her into elite sports. She no longer sees that possibility as a dream.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

"I will not let my daughter be an Olympic athlete," she said. "She will not be treated like this."

For more than 20 years, Jones pushed her body for Team USA. She raced through injuries, changed sports and represented the country in both the Summer and Winter Games.

When her body finally forced her to ask for help, she says the system treated her pain as a disciplinary problem.

"I’ve given so much to Team USA and represented this country as best I can," Jones said. "And when I needed Team USA back, they absolutely abandoned me."

World.title: Florida deputy killed ex-girlfriend over a TV, then himself, sheriff says
World.content:

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

A Florida sheriff’s deputy, honored multiple times for his bravery, dedication and compassion, killed a former girlfriend and then himself Monday after an argument over a television.

The victim was identified by friends as Mandy Fackler, who leaves behind two children, 12 and 9, Fox Tampa reported.

Deputy Troy Savetz had been with the Pinellas County Sheriff’s Office for 14 years and was a member of the marine unit.

He and the victim had an "on-again-off-again, tumultuous relationship," Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri said in a news conference.

MISSOURI MOM OF 5 FATALLY SHOT WHILE BUYING SLUSHIES WITH CHILDREN; POLICE SEARCH FOR GUNMAN

Savetz, 47, was waiting outside Fackler's home when she and her children returned from a day at the beach at about 5:30 p.m. He brandished a gun and was angry about "wanting his TV set back," Gualtieri said.

When the victim tried to call 911, Savetz took her phone. That’s when she told her two children to go inside.

They did as they were told. And they never saw her again.

The children were "extremely brave," calling 911 and giving dispatchers everything needed to identify the suspect, Pasco County Sheriff Chris Nocco told reporters.

When authorities arrived at the home, they saw the mother’s vehicle with the door wide open, and they found her phone, Nocco said.

"At that point, they realize that she's no longer there" at the residence, he said.

Officers sprang into action using K-9 teams, drones and aviation units, searching for the vehicle Savetz was driving when he carried the victim away, Nocco said.

About 90 minutes after the altercation began, authorities found the vehicle in nearby Spring Hill. Officers approached with a drone and saw two people inside.

When they reached the car on foot, they found Savetz and his victim dead.

"We're not sure when and at what point" he killed her and himself, Nocco said.

The children, now with their biological father, were unharmed in the incident.

They "should be starting off this week getting ready for school," Nocco said. Instead, they’re "starting off this week getting ready for a sad life without their mother."

He praised the children for their bravery and obedience at such a critical moment.

"I know eventually there's going to be a point in your life where you're going to go back and listen to all the videos and read all the reports," Nocco said.

"So please hear this directly from us: We listened to that 911 tape, and we know that your mother said to go inside to save your lives and to call 911. You did exactly what your mom asked you to do.

"Know this: Your mom is looking down from heaven, and she's so proud of you two … So know that you two did the right thing."

Nocco said officers were "amazed" by the children’s "calmness." The information they provided allowed for the fastest possible response.

"So we're so proud of you, and I know your mom is. But know [that] this entire community is praying for you."

OFF-DUTY TROOPER AND ARMED CITIZEN HAILED AS HEROES AFTER RETURNING FIRE ON IN-N-OUT GUNMAN

Before this, Savetz had earned accolades for his behavior while wearing the badge. In 2014, he was honored by the sheriff’s office for his "heroic action" in saving the life of a 24-year-old man, stopping him from jumping off a bridge in Pinellas County.

That earned him attention from the Tampa Bay Rays baseball team, who called him "Our Everyday MVP" in a June 2015 social media post. Wearing his green uniform, Savetz was honored by receiving the opportunity to throw out a ceremonial first pitch.

He was hailed a "hero" at local fundraisers and by radio stations.

In 2018, the sheriff’s office shared a social media post about how Savetz had adopted a pot-bellied pig he found while on duty. That year, he and Maple, as she became known, went on to be named ambassadors for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals in Tampa Bay.

But the "inexcusable" behavior of Savetz immediately ended his identity as a law enforcement officer, Gualtieri said.

World.title: Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman advance to GOP Senate primary runoff in South Carolina
World.content:
Appointed Sen. Darline Graham was forced into a Republican Senate primary runoff by Rep. Ralph Norman on Tuesday, raising the prospect that GOP voters will again reject a candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump.

Graham, who was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster to fill the remainder of her late brother Lindsey Graham’s term in July, is looking to also take his place on the November ballot for a full six years in the Senate. Trump encouraged her to run and then endorsed her in a primary that featured 10 GOP candidates, including Norman, Rep. Russell Fry and former Gov. Mark Sanford.

Rep. Ralph Norman in the U.S. Capitol in March. Tom Williams / Getty Images

The winner of the Aug. 25 runoff will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a doctor who won her party’s primary in June.

Graham, the first woman ever to represent South Carolina in the Senate, has never held elected office before, and her thin résumé appeared to cost her with some voters in the first round of the primary, calling into question the power of Trump’s imprimatur.

“I understand that she’s lost a brother and lost someone very special to her, and I sympathize with that, but at the same time, I don’t think that it’s necessary just to give it to her,” Republican voter Bob Howell told NBC News in Lexington, South Carolina.

Asked about Trump endorsing Graham, Howell said, “I like President Trump, but I don’t think that that’s necessarily what sways my vote.”

Earlier this year, Trump’s favored candidate for governor, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, got pushed into a runoff against state Attorney General Alan Wilson. Trump then issued a rare dual endorsement of both candidates in the Republican primary runoff, which Wilson won. That was one of several races across the country this year in which Trump’s preferred candidate failed to win the Republican nomination for a high office.

The winner of this Republican runoff will be heavily favored to prevail in November in a state where a Democrat has not won a Senate seat since Fritz Hollings’ re-election in 1998.

Graham, 62, replaced her older brother in the Senate after Lindsey Graham died July 11, after emergency personnel responded to a “cardiac arrest” call at his Capitol Hill home. The elder Graham had been seeking a fifth term in November and had already won a competitive primary in June.

Trump wasted little time in throwing his weight behind the younger Graham, issuing his “complete and total endorsement” on Truth Social on July 17, less than a week after her brother’s death.

Rep. Russell Fry in Charleston. Bill Clark / Getty Images

In her brief tenure in the Senate, Graham has been centrally involved in one issue: passage of a measure, earlier this month, that would impose new sanctions on Russia and Iran. Lindsey Graham had been the chief proponent of an earlier version of the legislation, which focused on applying pressure to Russia. At Trump’s request, Iran provisions were added before the Senate renamed the measure for Lindsey Graham and passed it, 86-11.

“I think I’ve accomplished a whole lot in three weeks,” Graham said after she cast her vote Tuesday, pointing to the sanctions bill and her vote to confirm Attorney General Todd Blanche. “I’m not being handed the seat. I realize that I have to earn votes, so I’m working really hard to do that.”

Graham added that she expected the race to move to a runoff.

Norman, who finished a distant third in the state’s Republican gubernatorial primary earlier this year, consistently supports Trump’s agenda in Congress. But Lindsey Graham was one of the president’s closest allies — Trump eulogized the late senator during a service at Washington National Cathedral — and that loyalty was reciprocated in the endorsement of Graham.

Now, with most of the state’s Republican voters having cast ballots for her rivals, Graham will need to consolidate support quickly in order to keep a seat that has been in her family since 2003.

World.title: Minnesota GOP picks Lisa Demuth over Trump-backed Mike Lindell for governor against Democrat Amy Klobuchar
World.content:
Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth won the Republican primary for governor, NBC News projects, defeating Trump ally Mike Lindell and setting up a general election matchup against Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar.

Demuth’s victory was an upset over Lindell, the MyPillow founder and election conspiracy theorist. Lindell had been leading in limited public polling heading into Election Day, and President Donald Trump endorsed him.

But attacks on Lindell from fellow Republicans — including questions about his residency raised by the chairman of the Minnesota Republican Party — hampered his campaign in the final weeks before the primary, as members of the Minnesota GOP sought a nominee who could beat Klobuchar in the general election.

Mike Lindell at the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora, N.D., on July 1. Leigh Vogel / Getty Images

Lindell has faced several legal challenges since 2020, when he championed Trump’s debunked theories about the 2020 presidential election, which former President Joe Biden won.

At a Minnesota Farmfest forum this month, Klobuchar appeared alongside three GOP candidates for governor and accused each of them of being “a rubber stamp of Donald Trump.”

Demuth and other Republicans — including Trump — have attacked Democrats in the blue state over two sprawling fraud scandals involving Medicaid and pandemic aid. Among the allegations were that hundreds of millions of dollars that had been earmarked for welfare programs were stolen.

At the farm event, Demuth blamed “incompetent Democrat control” for the fraud cases, and she has pointed on the campaign trail to the Fraud Prevention Agency Oversight Committee, which she established leading the state House.

In January, Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, who had planned to run for a third term, decided to drop his re-election campaign, citing the attacks over the fraud cases. A few weeks later, Klobuchar launched her campaign. She is one of four senators to run for governor this year.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., at the U.S. Capitol in May. Heather Diehl / Getty Images

Still, Republicans will have to overcome political trends in Minnesota in November to win the Governor’s Residence. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris won the state by about 4 percentage points in the most recent presidential election, when Walz was her running mate.

World.title: Democratic Rep. John Larson loses his primary to opponent calling for generational change
World.content:
Democratic Rep. John Larson of Connecticut has lost his primary race to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, NBC News projects, becoming the latest example of Democratic voters’ push to sweep out incumbent House members and replace them with younger leadership.

See live results here

Larson, 78, has been a fixture in Connecticut politics, having served for more than a decade in the state Legislature and almost three decades in Congress. A former member of party leadership, he touted his work on Social Security in Congress and had been backed by the state’s congressional delegation, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and key unions.

Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin speaks in July. Jessica Hill / AP

But Bronin, 47, mounted a serious campaign against him, calling for generational change and arguing that President Donald Trump’s second term called for new energy and new direction from Democratic lawmakers. Bronin raised more money than Larson and won over party activists at the state convention, winning the state party’s endorsement.

Larson is the 10th House member to lose a primary this year: seven Democrats and three Republicans.

“In this moment, when Donald Trump is president, the job of a member of Congress isn’t just in the subcommittee rooms, it’s what you are doing outside the walls of the Capitol to build a movement,” Bronin said in a late May interview.

“Over these next two years, it’s so important to have Democratic members of Congress using that platform not just to give red-faced speeches to an empty chamber for the C-SPAN cameras, but to ... carry our message, to win people back who lost faith in our party.”

Congressman John Larson exits a press conference at the Legislative Office Building, March 6, 2026, Hartford, Ct. Mark Mirko / Connecticut Public Broadcasting / Getty Images

Asked Monday on NBC News’ “Meet the Press Now” about the movement for generational change in the Democratic Party, Larson said that “I think the change that we need is to continue to go after Donald Trump” and touted his “record of doing that.”

“I have the endorsement of more elected officials, every sitting member in the congressional delegation, because they understand what I’ve been able to deliver,” he said. “They understand that they’re able to work with me, and they understand what I’ve been able to accomplish on their behalf. Luke Bronin has no record. I’m running on a record of accomplishment and achievement.”

Bronin replied that Larson has been in office “for about 50 years, and for the last 10 years or so, I just think he’s gotten stuck in a routine. And I understand, you know, it’s hard to find anybody who does the same thing for 30 years and doesn’t get a little bit stuck in the routine, but this is not a moment that we can keep doing the same thing.”

World.title: Los Angeles Lakers sold to Bob Iger, Josh Kushner for $12 billion
World.content:
The Los Angeles Lakers are being sold to an ownership group led by Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, the businessmen confirmed to NBC News on Wednesday.

The deal for the storied franchise had a $12 billion price tag, a person familiar with the matter said.

“As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world,” they said.

“We have immense respect for the leadership and vision of Jerry and Jeanie Buss. Our long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles.”

ESPN first reported the sale.

The Lakers were previously sold to businessman Mark Walter in October 2025 for a valuation of approximately $10 billion.

“Owning the Los Angeles Lakers has been one of the great honors of my life,” Walter said in a statement to NBC News. “It has been an extraordinary investment, but what I will carry with me is the community, the fans, and a city that treats this team as family. I am grateful to Jeanie Buss, the Buss family, the players, and the staff for welcoming me into this chapter. The Lakers belong to Los Angeles, and I have every confidence the best is still ahead.”

The Lakers are one of the most iconic franchises in sports with 17 championships, most recently in 2020. Last season, the team finished fourth in the Western Conference before being eliminated by the Oklahoma City Thunder in the semifinals.

NBA superstar LeBron James, the all-time leading scorer in the league, played eight seasons in Los Angeles. He announced in July he was leaving to join the Philadelphia 76ers on a two-year, two-year, $8 million contract. The team will now be led by six-time NBA All-Star Luka Dončić, who was No. 1 the league with 33.5 points per game last season.

Kushner is the founder of venture firm Thrive Capital, co-founder of Oscar Health and a minority owner of the NBA’s Miami Heat. FIFA wanted to sell a minority stake in the World Cup to Thrive Capital, but the plan was halted amid worldwide backlash from soccer leaders in Europe, North America and Asia.

Kushner is the younger brother of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

World.title: Los Angeles Lakers to be sold to Bob Iger, Josh Kushner for $12.5 billion
World.content:
For the second time in about a year, the Los Angeles Lakers will be sold to new ownership for a record fee in professional sports.

Former Walt Disney Company CEO Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner, the founder of venture capital firm Thrive Capital, have agreed to purchase the iconic NBA franchise from Mark Walter, Chief Executive Officer of Guggenheim Partners, the pair confirmed to CBS LA.

The fee is $12.5 billion, sources familiar with the deal told CBS LA.

"As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world," Iger and Kushner said in a joint statement. "We have immense respect for the leadership and vision of Jerry and Jeanie Buss. Our long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles."

NEW YORK, NY - SEPTEMBER 2: Adam Silver, Joshua Kushner and Bob Iger are seen on Day 10 of the 2025 US Open Tennis Championships at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on September 2, 2025 in Flushing Meadows, Queens, New York City. (Photo by XNY/Star Max/GC Images) XNY/Star Max

The stunning deal comes about 14 months after Walter purchased a majority stake in the team for about $10 billion, a then-record fee, from the Buss family. Jeanie Buss, daughter of the late Jerry, retained her position as Lakers governor despite last year's deal, but it's unclear what her role, if any, will be going forward under new ownership. Before last year's sale to Walter, the previous record was last year's $6.1 billion sale of the Lakers' rival Boston Celtics.

It's the second venture into pro sports for the 75-year-old Iger, who in 2024 purchased NWSL's LA franchise, Angel City FC, along with his wife, journalist Willow Bay. He served two tenures as Disney's CEO, first from 2005 to 2020 and again from 2022 until this March.

Kushner, 41, is the youngest son of U.S. Ambassador to France and Monaco Charles Kushner and brother of Jared, the son-in-law of President Trump. Joshua had purchased a minority stake in the Miami Heat last year.

The Lakers' sale comes as the NBA seeks ownership bids for expansion franchises in Seattle and Las Vegas. The addition of two new teams would bring the league's total to 32 franchises.

On the court, the Lakers' new era will be led by superstar guard Luka Doncic, who was acquired in a shocking trade from the Dallas Mavericks in Feb. 2025. Doncic signed a contract extension with the franchise last August.

The new-look Lakers will also have to deal with the loss of one of the greatest players in league history, LeBron James, who left in free agency this summer. He announced last month that he'd finish his career as a member of the Philadelphia 76ers.

World.title: NYC probes prediction markets over advertising practices
World.content:
The New York City Council said Wednesday that it is investigating four prediction markets over allegations that the companies engage in deceptive marketing.

The probe will examine the advertising practices of Gemini Titan, Kalshi and Polymarket, all of which are based in New York, as well as Texas-based Coinbase.

"Prediction markets aggressively entice consumers to bet and wager on sports, politics, culture, weather and pretty much anything," New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in a statement. "We refuse to let New Yorkers, especially our young people, become collateral damage."

A Polymarket  in a subway station in New York on Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026. Michael Nagle / Bloomberg via Getty Images

As part of the investigation, Menin has requested information from the platforms about their marketing practices in New York.

Prediction markets allow users to wager on sports, political elections and many other events.

The probe comes after a June investigation by the Wall Street Journal uncovered that Polymarket paid online content creators to post videos that misrepresented their earnings from trades. In response, the platform said it would conduct an audit of its promotional content.

On Monday, the New York City Council said it would also investigate these allegations against Polymarket, including claims that the company targets younger adults using false and deceptive marketing.

"We look forward to engaging with the New York City Council on this matter," Polymarket said in a statement.

The other companies subject to the investigation didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

New York City's probe highlights the broader turf battle between states and the federal government over who should have regulatory control over prediction markets. Multiple states have filed lawsuits against the platforms, including New York, where Attorney General Letitia James has sued Coinbase, Gemini Titan and Kalshi, accusing them of running illegal gambling operations that flout state laws.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that oversees prediction markets, has filed lawsuits seeking to block states from tightening rules governing them. The agency argues that Congress gives it exclusive jurisdiction over the regulation of derivative markets.

Yet attorneys note that it remains legally murky whether the CFTC's jurisdiction extends to sports betting, which drives much of the trading volume on prediction markets.

World.title: Rubio, Bessent took decoy Air Force One, Hegseth flew on secret flight with Trump
World.content:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent were on a decoy flight last month when President Trump secretly took a different plane from the publicly identified Air Force One aircraft from the NATO summit, according to sources familiar with the situation.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was on the secret flight with Mr. Trump out of Turkey. White House aides Natalie Harp, Walt Nauta and Dan Scavino were also on catering truck and the flight with Mr. Trump.

Rubio and Bessent, who separated and maintained the line of succession, were aware the president was on another, secret plane. Several other White House aides were on the decoy flight, including Stephen Miller, Will Scharf, Steven Cheung, Mike Needham, Ross Worthington and Monica Crowley.

While the plane the president is traveling on is supposed to be identified as Air Force One, the decoy flight was publicly identified as Air Force One.

July 8, 2026: This photo shows the other aircraft in the background, which President Trump reportedly took to U.K. Note: The catering truck in this photo at the rear of the plane in the foreground is not believed to be the one that covertly transported the president. This photo was taken at 8:26 p.m. local time, Ankara, Turkey. ABC News pool photo / Ena Suto

On July 8, Mr. Trump announced he would leave Ankara in the old Air Force One rather than a newer Qatari-donated jet that he had taken to the NATO summit. The president said he was switching planes "for old time's sake," and U.S. forces stationed at a British refueling stop would be able to check out the new plane, but CBS News has reported that the Secret Service advised he take the older plane for security reasons.

With the help of a catering truck, Mr. Trump covertly moved from the publicly identified Air Force One to the other plane.

Mr. Trump told CBS News' Nancy Cordes on Tuesday night that the decision to take the secret flight was made by the military and Secret Service, who "wanted me to go in a different flight."

Mr. Trump said it was in response to a threat, which he called unsurprising, noting that he gets "a lot of threats."

"Any consequential president has a lot of threats," Mr. Trump told reporters.

Asked why it was too dangerous for him to fly on Air Force One, but not members of the press, he said: "I think, actually, the plane that I flew on was at greater risk."

Video footage captured by the press showed the president walking up the stairs of the old Air Force One and disappearing into the plane, with a catering truck visible on the other side of the jet. Several minutes later, the truck pulled away and drove off to another U.S. government plane, which The Washington Post reported was an Air Force C-32A. The Washington Post first reported the secret plane trip, which had not been publicly disclosed until then.

Mr. Trump then flew from Ankara to a refueling stop in the United Kingdom on the separate plane while members of the press and the president's staff traveled the same route on Air Force One — and believed they were on board the same aircraft as the president.

While in Ankara, members of the press were told to keep the window shades in Air Force One's press cabin closed, reporters said at the time. Asked why the shades needed to be closed, Mr. Trump later told reporters they were "probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags that we have to deal with."

In the U.K., Mr. Trump switched to the newer Air Force One, which was donated by the government of Qatar last year and retrofitted by the U.S. Air Force to serve as the new presidential plane. Mr. Trump spoke to members of the press while they flew across the Atlantic toward Washington, D.C.

The White House said in July that the Qatari-donated plane would be undergoing security upgrades, which Mr. Trump said would be "maxed out."

World.title: Watch Live: Lindsay Clancy jury hearing from mental health counselor
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy's trial entered a 12th day Wednesday. The jury is hearing testimony from Latiesha Dukes, a mental health counselor who worked with Clancy.

You can watch the trial in Plymouth Superior Court live on CBS News Boston in the embedded video or on YouTube when court is in session.

Clancy, 36, is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. She has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham said Clancy planned the murders and faked a suicide attempt.

Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington said Clancy admits to killing her children but says she should not be held criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Lindsay Clancy in Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts on August 11, 2026. Jonathan Wiggs/Boston Globe Staff/Pool

Massachusetts State Police investigator testifies

Earlier, Sgt. Dan Lawlor testified. Lawlor has worked for Massachusetts State Police for nine years.

The night of the children's deaths, Lawlor went to South Shore Hospital in Weymouth and saw Clancy, who was unable to speak and suffering from injuries after jumping out a second-floor window.

Lawlor went to Boston Children's Hospital to check on 8-month-old Callan's status, then later went to Brigham and Women's Hospital, where Clancy was transferred, to stand watch outside the room.

Reddington took over cross-examination after about 15 minutes. The defense attorney asked Lawlor about how no one was allowed to get into Clancy's hospital room. Eventually, Reddington got a court order for psychologist Paul Zeizel to enter the room to meet with Clancy.

"Isn't it fair to say that one of the contentions of the district attorneys is that Paul Ziezel, my doctor, that I got a court order to get in and see her, told her to call Pat and tell him that she heard voices?" Reddington asked.

When Reddington referred to Pat, he was speaking about Patrick Clancy. Lindsay and Patrick Clancy were married at the time of their children's deaths, but have since divorced.

Following that question, the judge asked to see attorneys at sidebar due to an objection by the prosecution. After about 20 minutes, the judge sent jurors out of the room to question Lawlor without the jury present.

With the jury out of the room, Reddington asked about Lawlor's recollection that lead investigator Josh McKelligan had told him that at some point when Clancy was hospitalized, she called Patrick to indicate she was hearing voices. Reddington suggested that the theory investigators were trying to use was that Ziezel had suggested Clancy make the phone call.

"I don't know if it's a theory or not, I just recall the conversation," Lawlor said.

The prosecutor then questioned Lawlor without the jury present.

"You never had a conversation with the prosecution about what the theory was, did you?" she asked. Lawlor said he had not, saying it was only with the fellow trooper.

"Is this conversation guiding your testimony?" Buckingham asked. Lawlor said it was not.

The judge took arguments under advisement and the jury returned a short time later.

With the jury back in the room, Reddington asked Lawlor if he and McKelligan talked about the theory that Ziezel "is the reason that she told her husband she heard voices." Lawlor said they did talk about that theory.

"There's no investigator basis for that, that's McKelligan's speculation, correct?" Reddington asked. Lawlor said that was correct.

Buckingham then questioned Lawlor.

"Is it fair to say you oftentimes will have conversations as investigations are unfolding with other investigators that you're working on the case with about the case, potential evidence, theories of the case?" Buckingham asked.

Lawlor said that was true, and added that theories can change over time.

Buckingham asked Lawlor, "You didn't hear anything that occurred in that room that day that you were there when Dr. ZIezel was there, did you?"

"I did not hear anything," Lawlor said, concluding his testimony at around 10:45 a.m.

Lindsay Clancy trial

The jury heard from a psychiatric nurse practitioner Tuesday who specializes in postpartum patients. Rebecca Jollotta said she met with Clancy three times late in 2022, a few weeks before the murders. Jollotta was the 62nd witness in the trial.

Judge William Sullivan said the attorneys told him the proceedings are "well on schedule and somewhat ahead of schedule."

If convicted of first-degree murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If the jury finds that she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, she will be sent to a state psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts.

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: Inflation just fell again. Is that good news for mortgage rates?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

Cooling inflation could change the outlook for mortgage rates, but several factors remain in play. J Studios/Getty Images

Prospective homebuyers finally received some encouraging inflation news this week. After months of stubborn price growth, the latest inflation report offered another sign that some of those pressures may be easing. The Consumer Price Index rose 3.4% annually in July, down slightly from 3.5% in June and more noticeably from the 4.2% rate recorded in May. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, also edged lower, dropping from 2.6% in June to 2.5% in July.

Those declines arrive at an important time for prospective homebuyers. Mortgage rates remain elevated, with the average 30-year fixed rate at 6.75% as of August 12 — which is significantly higher than the sub-3% mortgage rates that were available at the start of the decade. But with the Federal Reserve weighing both inflation trends and changes in the labor market, each new economic report has the potential to impact where borrowing costs head from here.

That makes the latest inflation figures particularly relevant for those planning to buy a home or refinance one soon. Understanding how the latest inflation decline fits into the broader economic picture can help borrowers understand what could happen to mortgage rates next — and whether this latest inflation news is as encouraging as it appears.

Find out how affordable the right mortgage loan could be today.

Is the inflation drop good news for mortgage rates?

Falling inflation is generally an encouraging sign for mortgage rates, but that doesn't mean home loan rates will immediately drop every time inflation does. That's because mortgage rates are influenced by several parts of the economy, and inflation is only one of those driving factors.

Inflation matters in this equation because mortgage rates are closely connected to what's happening in the bond market — particularly with the 10-year Treasury yield. When inflation is high or appears likely to stay high, investors typically want higher returns on long-term bonds to make up for the fact that inflation reduces the purchasing power of the money they'll receive in the future. That can push Treasury yields higher, and mortgage rates often move higher alongside them.

And the reverse can happen when inflation cools. If investors become more confident that price growth is slowing, Treasury yields may fall, giving mortgage rates room to move lower, too. So the July CPI report, which showed inflation declining for the second consecutive month, is a potentially positive development for mortgage loan borrowers.

The latest inflation figures could also affect expectations for the Federal Reserve. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but its decisions can influence the financial markets that do. When inflation is running too high, the Fed typically has less flexibility to cut its benchmark interest rate. As inflation moves closer to the Fed's 2% target, however, policymakers may have more room to lower rates, particularly if other economic conditions support doing so.

Inflation isn't the only economic indicator pointing to a potential shift, though. The latest jobs report showed employers cut 23,000 jobs in July, a much weaker result than economists had anticipated. Signs that the labor market is weakening, combined with cooling inflation, could increase expectations for lower Fed rates. If investors begin to expect declining borrowing costs, mortgage rates could start responding even before the Fed actually makes a move.

Still, that doesn't guarantee a significant mortgage rate drop is around the corner. Inflation remains above the Fed's 2% goal despite the recent declines, and one or two favorable reports aren't enough to establish where the economy is headed.

For homebuyers, the July inflation report is better viewed as one piece of a much larger puzzle. If inflation continues falling and the labor market continues to soften, the conditions for lower mortgage rates could improve. But the next inflation and employment reports — along with how financial markets react to them — will help further determine whether mortgage rates actually move meaningfully lower.

Learn more about the mortgage loan rates you could qualify for now.

How to find a low mortgage rate in today's market

With mortgage rates still hovering well above 6%, even a relatively small difference in the rate you're offered can have a meaningful impact on your monthly payment and total borrowing costs. In turn, it makes sense to focus on the factors you can control rather than trying to perfectly time the broader rate market.

Start by shopping around with several mortgage lenders. Rates, fees and loan terms can vary significantly from one lender to another, even for the same borrower. Getting quotes from at least three to five lenders can make it easier to identify the most competitive combination of rate and closing costs.

It can also pay to strengthen your borrower profile before applying. A higher credit score, lower debt-to-income ratio and larger down payment can make you less risky in a lender's eyes, potentially helping you qualify for better terms. Paying down revolving credit card balances, correcting credit report errors and avoiding new debt before applying for a mortgage can also help.

You should also compare more than just the advertised interest rate. Review each loan's annual percentage rate (APR), which incorporates certain borrowing costs and can provide a clearer picture of what you're paying. If you expect to remain in the home long enough to recoup the upfront expense, buying mortgage points to lower your rate may be worth considering.

Don't overlook different loan types, either. Depending on your finances and eligibility, government-backed mortgages or adjustable-rate mortgage loans could offer lower initial rates than certain conventional fixed-rate options. Just make sure the loan structure fits your long-term plans rather than choosing it based solely on the starting rate.

The bottom line

The July inflation report provides another indication that the sharp price pressures seen earlier this year may be easing, and that could ultimately create a more favorable backdrop for mortgage rates. But mortgage rates don't move based on inflation alone, and with inflation still above the Fed's target and economic uncertainty remaining elevated, you shouldn't count on a dramatic decline in rates in the near term. If you're ready to buy a home, however, you could benefit from comparing multiple lenders and strengthening your financial profile now.

World.title: Zhu Rongji, who drove China's 1990s economic reforms, has died at 97
World.content:
Zhu Rongji, who drove China's 1990s economic reforms, has died at 97

Enlarge this image toggle caption K.Y. Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images K.Y. Cheng/South China Morning Post via Getty Images

Zhu Rongji, former premier of China, has died at age 97. The cause of death was given as illness, according to state media.

Zhu, an acerbic technocrat and a trained engineer, was renowned for far-reaching economic reforms throughout the 1990s that sought to transition China from the chaos of its post-Maoist years to a more global market-oriented financial system, without completely ceding the Communist Party's control over the economy.

Despite staying almost completely out of the public eye after retiring from the premiership in 2003, he remains both loved and reviled in the country indelibly shaped by him. His reform legacy remains contested in China; in freeing up the country's enormous labor and financial resources, he helped to create vast amounts of wealth over the next three decades while also seeding institutions with future vulnerabilities.

Sponsor Message

"From the point of view of a policymaker, [he] embraced the notion of a China whose economic system was more compatible with that of the West. And by compatible, I mean vastly reformed, more open, less state-dominated, very limited state intervention," said Charlene Barshefsky, a lawyer and former U.S. trade representative who sat across the negotiating table from Zhu over years-long talks to let China enter the World Trade Organization (WTO).

In order to join the WTO, China first needed to get preferential trading status with the United States — which in turn demanded hard concessions and that it open up its closed economy to American companies. Zhu was under huge pressure to find compromise, and he let his views be known.

Enlarge this image toggle caption Joyce Naltchayan/AFP via Getty Images Joyce Naltchayan/AFP via Getty Images

In 2000, the U.S. Senate voted to give China that preferential trading status, and the following year, China joined the WTO. The agreement was a windfall for the nascent Chinese economy. The country became an export powerhouse, and foreign businesses rushed to China to establish a foothold.

The 6 1/2-year process let Zhu show off his flinty personality, though he struck U.S. officials as inquisitive and flexible. "This was not talking points. It was a lot of give and take," said Kenneth Lieberthal, a China expert who was a national security adviser for then-President Bill Clinton. He met Zhu multiple times during the negotiations.

Sponsor Message

Zhu was born in 1928 in the city of Changsha, in China's Hunan province. He graduated from Beijing's Tsinghua University, where he was also chosen as president of the student union, with a degree in electrical engineering, the winter before the Communist Party won control over China. In October 1949, when the new Communist-led republic was founded, Zhu officially joined the Chinese Communist Party.

His blunt, say-it-like-it-is style got him in trouble

Zhu's father died before he was born, and his mother died when he was 9 years old. Being an orphan, the need to survive helped shape his strong personality: thick-skinned and extremely direct.

"My defining characteristic is independent thought," he told bureaucrats in 1987, right before becoming mayor of Shanghai. "I say what I think."

When Chinese troops fatally fired on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989, Zhu did not issue the standard propaganda line denying the tragedy. "The event that occurred recently in Beijing is a historical fact, and historical facts cannot be covered up by anybody. The truth will always come out," he wrote in an essay published in a Shanghai newspaper.

His blunt, say-it-like-it-is style got him in serious trouble. In 1958, he was labeled an ideological "rightist" and briefly expelled from the party for criticizing Chairman Mao Zedong's economic policies, but managed to hold on to a job in state planning. In 1970, he was purged again during the Cultural Revolution and sent to do five years of manual labor at a party reeducation school.

Zhu was rehabilitated after Mao died in 1976 and Deng Xiaoping came to power as China's leader. Zhu then worked his way back up the bureaucratic ladder with the same pragmatism he had learned as an engineer.

"Regardless of what country your company is from, when you arrive in China, you should receive fair and equal treatment. I just want you to pay taxes," he joked in 1999 to an audience of American businessmen, explaining that China was open for foreign investment.

Sponsor Message

A career state planner, Zhu nevertheless quickly adjusted to the economic chaos of the 1990s, as China careened between capitalism and state-led socialism. As central bank governor, Zhu successfully tamed runaway inflation. While vice premier, he also led a dramatic centralization of the tax system that incentivized land sales and huge wealth creation, along with hugely unsustainable levels of debt.

After being appointed premier in 1998, he entered office with a bold promise: He would reform the indebted state banks within two years and inefficient state enterprises within three. That earned him both instant enemies and fans.

"No matter whether what lies ahead is a minefield or a bottomless abyss, I will carry out my duties until the last breath in my body," he vowed.

Zhu's most controversial legacy by far remains restructuring China's bloated state-owned enterprises. He axed smaller, inefficient companies, leaving an estimated 30 million state workers suddenly jobless.

Worker protests erupted all over China. Zhu had the willpower — or callousness, as his critics would say — to ignore them.

"The central government decided that the laid-off worker problem could just be ignored and forgotten," said Dorothy Solinger, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of California, Irvine, who studies migrant labor in China.

Zhu tried to offset the layoffs' impacts. He created a basic social welfare system that exists to this day and made steps to boost basic health care, which had crumbled in rural areas. But pockets of China, especially in the northeast region of the country, where workers were reliant on state employment in heavy industry sectors, never fully recovered economically.

"I think their children also have a problem because they miss out on the things that the better-off part of the population could do, such as hiring tutors or going on extracurricular activities, going to the better schools," said Solinger. "It's a growing underclass."

Sponsor Message

Zhu took the criticism in stride. Unlike most Communist leaders, who read off staid and carefully prepared scripts, he loved engaging with and ad-libbing to the press.

"He loved answering all the questions, no matter how tough or sensitive," remembered Rose Luqiu, a former journalist for Hong Kong outlet Phoenix News who spent 10 years covering Zhu during his international state visits. "The only way he refused to answer was using a quite humorous way to dodge the questions."

His gallows humor allowed him to weather intense periods of criticism from senior ideologues within the Communist Party, once quipping during an anti-corruption campaign: "I have prepared 100 coffins: 99 for the corrupt officials and one for myself."

Other reforms of his did not materialize, in part because an austere Zhu never managed to cultivate the political patronage networks that would have allowed him to overcome fierce opposition within party ranks to his proposals. His efforts to reduce bad debt at China's state banks and reform the pension system floundered.

Enlarge this image toggle caption Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images Greg Baker/AFP via Getty Images

Zhu "represented really a different time, a different era for China"

Zhu is now invoked with pleasant nostalgia. Under China's current leader, Xi Jinping, the country became more nationalistic, more beholden to the state and more closed off to the outside world.

"I think that Zhu Rongji represented really a different time, a different era for China: the time when China wanted to find its way in what, due to that time, was the best possible way, which was to move towards Western-style economics, to move toward Western-style rules," said Barshefsky, the former U.S. trade negotiator.

Zhu Rongji spent the last years of his life at his Beijing home in the western hills of the Chinese capital. He loved Peking Opera and spent much of his days listening to music — and quietly advising some of the newest generation of technocrats running China, though not all appear to have listened to him.

World.title: B.C. officials 'can't even think about' lifting Summerland evacuation orders until wildfire under control

The Latest:

Regional officials said they have heard frustration from families who evacuated their homes in Summerland, B.C., but said they "can't even think about" lifting evacuation orders until the Bald Range fire is better controlled.

Temporary access permits to Summerland are being triaged, with utility crews getting priority to ensure utilities can adequately sustain the community.

The B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) reminds people to stay clear of the Bonanza Creek wildfire, as it's a popular recreational area surrounded by numerous provincial parks.

of the Bonanza Creek wildfire, as it's a popular recreational area surrounded by numerous provincial parks. The province issued yellow and orange air quality warnings for regions across the central and southern Interior.

Bald Range wildfire still burning out of control

During a Tuesday livestream from the Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen, Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes said they cannot consider lifting evacuation orders or alerts until the Bald Range wildfire is under control.

A BCWS update on Tuesday said overnight recoveries were poor due to clear skies and fuels remain "exceptionally dry and highly receptive to fire."

Officials say the volatile nature of the wildfire challenges their ability to plan ahead, as they are still responding to the fire as it progresses.

Ground crews are pictured battling the Bald Range fire overnight on Aug. 7, 2026. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

"We have to make sure it's safe," said Holmes.

Until then, temporary access permits are being granted in some circumstances.

Permits are "basically triaged," according to Deborah Jones-Middleton, the protective services manager with the district. She said utilities professionals, for example, will be permitted into the area as long, as it's safe to do so, to ensure utilities are adequately running to sustain a community.

There were 100 firefighters from Mexico battling the Bald Range fire on Tuesday, bringing the total number of ground personnel to 193. Heavy equipment, aviation personnel continue to construct control lines, while structure protection is in place around the community.

Brunswick Complex nears another highway

As of Tuesday afternoon, the Ainslie Creek wildfire had scorched roughly 614 square kilometres of land, and its northeastern edge was only about three kilometres west of Highway 8, which runs through Merritt.

The northeast edge of the wildfire is roughly 20 kilometres northwest of Merritt. The BCWS noted the Ainslie Creek fire hasn't crossed control lines or entered the community.

As a result of the growing fire, the Lower Nicola Indian Band expanded its evacuation alert to cover all properties in the Nicola Mameet Indian Reserve No. 1. It also issued an evacuation order for a property on its Speous Indian Reserve No. 8.

The BCWS said in its Tuesday update that the fire remains active along the northeast and southeast flanks, growing eastward throughout Monday. It added that as of Tuesday morning , the fire stopped about two kilometres short of control lines, and had not impacted Highway 8.

The Ainslie Creek wildfire has a pattern of showing aggressive behaviour and major growth, according to the service, when any two factors of elevated winds, low humidity and clear skies combine.

The Ainslie Creek fire burns along the Fraser River on July 27, 2026. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

The Brunswick Complex consists of the Brunswick Creek wildfire, burning on the east bank of the Fraser River above Boston Bar, and the Ainslie Creek wildfire, burning on its west bank. Highway 1 is directly affected by the wildfires and remains closed.

There were 236 firefighters, 20 helicopters, 59 pieces of heavy equipment and 85 structure protection personnel fighting the Brunswick Complex as of Tuesday.

Road closures

According to DriveBC , most of the major highway closures from previous days remain the same.

Due to the Bald Range wildfire, Highway 97 is closed between Peachland and the Pyramid Picnic Area in Kickininee Provincial Park. Traffic is being redirected to Highway 33.

Westside Road also remains closed due to the Bradley Creek Complex, burning on the west bank of Okanagan Lake, north of Penticton.

Other closures to Highway 1 north of Hope and Highway 97 north of Cache Creek remain in place.

World.title: Spain confronts influx of solar eclipse tourists while still battling wildfires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of thousands of tourists have descended on Spain in the hopes of experiencing Wednesday's solar eclipse.

But the celestial event comes amid elevated temperatures and an increased risk of wildfires in Spain, raising alarm bells for authorities hoping to ensure the boom in astrotourism doesn’t come with lasting fire damage.

"We've had an extremely tough summer in Spain, with yet another series of major forest fires. That's why we must restrict any kind of activity that could generate a spark," Virginia Barcones, secretary general for civil ​protection and emergencies at Spain's Interior Ministry, told Reuters.

A heat wave has been smothering much of Europe since May, and Spain is currently grappling with a devastating wildfire season. More than 603,000 acres (2,440 square kilometres) of land have been burned in around 400 fires so far this year, according to the European Forest ​Fire Information System.

To ensure that eclipse tourists don’t add to this number, authorities are deploying 35,000 officers on Wednesday to large, outdoor gatherings in the hopes of spotting and stopping any new fires that may start, according to Barcones.

Forest rangers work in a wildfire-scorched area near Casillas, Avila province, Spain on July 30. (AP Photo/Olmo Calvo)

Spain is one of the best viewing locations for Wednesday's solar eclipse — the narrow band of totality, around 200 kilometres across, also crosses northern Russia, eastern Greenland and western Iceland, clipping the northeastern tip of Portugal and curving across a wide swathe of northern Spain, ending at the Balearic Islands. Around 15 million people live in its path, mostly in Spain.

Only those in the path of totality will witness the moon fully covering the sun. In Canada, a partial eclipse will be visible, with those on the east edge of Nunavut and Newfoundland seeing the most coverage. Authorities are reminding viewers to always use eclipse glasses to protect their eyes.

This will be the first time a full solar eclipse has been visible from mainland Spain in 120 years, and the excitement has sparked a flurry of travel.

WATCH | How and when to see the partial eclipse in Canada: Where will the partial solar eclipse be visible in Canada? | Duration 3:26 Parts of Europe will see a total solar eclipse on Wednesday. Canada's not so lucky, but parts of the country will get to see a partial eclipse.

Earlier this summer, authorities in Spain announced that special measures approved by the Ministry of the Interior would be in place for the solar eclipse to handle the large crowds anticipated. Searches for lodging along the eclipse’s path of totality spiked as the event grew nearer, according to Expedia Group, with Valencia, Spain, seeing a 245 per cent increase in searches compared to the previous year.

A total of 660 official viewing sites have been outlined by regional governments in the hopes of handling the expected influx of more than 440,000 people. Authorities estimate around 1.5 million people could be on the road during the day to head to viewing sites. Both national and local authorities are warning tourists against using barbecues or going into dry countryside where fire risk is higher.

Are you currently in or travelling to Europe to watch the solar eclipse? We want to hear from you. Send us your photos or videos and share your experience at ask@cbc.ca.

The eclipse is anticipated to contribute more than 347 million euros to Spain's economy, according to a July economic impact study by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business.

Dry conditions, fire fears

Three major wildfires are still burning in the provinces of Huelva, Segovia and Huesca. Only one of the severe blazes is in the path of totality, according to Joe McNorton, a scientist with the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts: the Las Peñas de Riglos wildfire active to the north of Zaragoza, which "could pose a danger if astro-tourists venture into the area."

Burnt trees stand in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Valencia province, Spain, on July 30. (Damian Torres/The Associated Press)

But the forest fire index across much of the Iberian Peninsula and the Balearic Islands is expected to reach "very high or extreme levels" on the day of the eclipse, according to AEMET , Spain's meteorological agency. And the country is perilously dry: last month, only 4.3 millimetres of rainfall was recorded across mainland Spain, a quarter of the normal precipitation expected this time of year. It was the driest July on record, according to AEMET.

"Around 90 per cent of wildfires are human-caused, so the presence of many more people in rural areas inevitably brings more potential ignition sources," McNorton told CBC News.

WATCH | Heat wave in Europe threatens to fuel further wildfires: Heat wave threatens to further fuel Europe’s wildfires | Duration 2:02 Wildfires in France have forced 4,000 more people along the Atlantic coast to evacuate as another heat wave threatens to fuel the flames there and in neighbouring Spain.

AEMET is forecasting temperatures upwards of 35 C on eclipse day, with some regions reaching 40 C, although peak temperatures will be down two to five degrees by the time of the eclipse.

Reykjavík, Iceland, will see totality at 5:48 p.m. local time, but viewers in Spain won’t see the eclipse enter totality until just before sunset, with northwestern Spain entering totality starting at around 8:28 p.m. local time. At its maximum, totality will last two minutes and 18 seconds, although this will vary by location.

Eclipse fervor holding

Even amid a heat wave and wildfires, eclipse travelers have not been deterred. Jan Cami, a professor in the physics and astronomy department at Western University in London, Ont., says he is unsurprised.

"It’s an event where you don't need to be a scientist at all to actually enjoy that this is an absolute spectacle that nature has provided for us," Cami told CBC News.

During maximum totality, the temperature drops, and stars and planets become briefly visible during the day, an experience so "overwhelming" that those who witness it often start making plans for their next trip to see it again, he said. He has colleagues both in Spain and on a cruise in Iceland waiting for their chance to see the sun vanish on Wednesday.

A view of totality during the solar eclipse on April 8, 2024, in Hot Springs National Park, Ark. (Nick Ingram/The Associated Press)

"I think [travelling for celestial events] is a great opportunity at the same time to learn about other parts of the world."

It’s this sense of shared meaning that Cami is hoping will touch tourists in Spain – that those who battle the heat to see the eclipse will reflect on the struggles of the country they’re in, and how far-reaching the impacts of climate change are.

Maarten Savelkoel, 76, from the Netherlands, visits a campsite to see the total solar eclipse, in Arija, Spain, on Tuesday. (Borja Suarez/Reuters)

The 2026 eclipse is just the first in a trio of solar eclipses in the next few years that will be visible from Spain. Two more are expected, on Aug. 2, 2027, and Jan. 26, 2028, respectively.

The 2027 solar eclipse could prompt even more astrotourism, Cami predicts. The path of totality will cross southern Spain before continuing to Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

"You can see the total eclipse of next year while [at] the pyramids of Giza," he said.

World.title: Manitoba mother whose 'little angel' died in CFS care says she was trying to get kids back
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A grieving mother says someone needs to be held accountable after her four-year-old daughter died in the care of Child and Family Services and her two other children were taken to a Winnipeg hospital with serious injuries.

Manitoba First Nations Police Service officers were called to a home in Long Plain First Nation on Sunday morning after the four-year-old was found by first responders with injuries and in medical distress, RCMP said in a news release Tuesday.

The girl was pronounced dead and her two sisters, a one-year-old and two-year-old, were taken to the hospital — one of them in critical condition.

Her mother said her four-year-old daughter was starting kindergarten in September and was about to celebrate her fifth birthday later this month.

"She was just a little angel. She loved her little siblings." the mom told CBC Tuesday. "She loved to sing, she loved to dance."

CBC is not identifying the mother to protect the identity of the two children who remain in the care of Child and Family Services.

RCMP Major Crimes Services said they took over the investigation from First Nations police due to the nature of the girl's death and the injuries to the siblings. No charges have been laid.

Children under care of CFS

The children were under the care of Waywayseecapo CFS, a western Manitoba agency based in Waywayseecapo First Nation, according to emails viewed by CBC.

A representative from Waywayseecapo CFS agency — which is under the umbrella of the Southern First Nations Network of Care authority — said the agency is not commenting on the death at this time.

The mom spent the last two days visiting her children at Health Sciences Centre's children's hospital.

"They're just babies and they're just sweethearts," said the girls' mother, who spoke to CBC Tuesday outside of the hospital.

The mother said her kids had been in care since October and the last time she saw them was in February.

At that time, she says they looked skinny and she could see bruising on one child's eyes — a concern she raised with her CFS worker.

"I had a gut feeling something was happening and nobody listened to me," she said.

Families minister to do internal investigation

Manitoba's Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine said her department will be doing its own internal investigation and they have reported the death to the Manitoba Advocate for Children and Youth to also investigate.

In an emailed statement, Fontaine said she is "deeply saddened by the tragic death of this young child."

She cannot comment further on the circumstances of the case due to the active RCMP investigation, she said.

Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine said the province will conduct its own internal investigation into the death. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

Her government remains committed to "working with the Southern Network of Care and all authorities to strengthen supports and ensure children and families receive the care and services they need," she said in the statement.

A spokesperson for the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 First Nations in southern Manitoba including Waywayseecappo First Nation, sent condolences to the family.

"Given the ongoing investigations into the circumstances surrounding the child’s death and the injuries sustained by the other children, SCO will not comment further or speculate at this time," the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

'Time to take my baby back in a casket'

After her kids were apprehended in October, the mom says she went into a four-week treatment program in December, took parenting classes and was hoping to get her kids back this summer.

"I did everything, I went to treatment, I did the programs, I stayed sober. I cleaned my house," she said.

"Then just nothing was done about it. And now look, time to take my baby back in a casket and my other girls are just so broken."

She is speaking about what happened to her daughter because she doesn't want to see another death in care and she wants answers as to how this happened.

"I just want her voice to be heard and make sure it doesn't happen to any other kids. Some things need to be done about this," she said.

"All I wanted was them to be home with me where they were safe. And nobody listened."

World.title: What to know about the trial of Lindsay Clancy, woman accused of killing her 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

The Lindsay Clancy murder trial is making headlines around the world as jurors hear harrowing details of the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children.

Clancy's legal team does not deny that she killed her children, but is arguing she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill — in the grip of bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis, a rare condition that the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health says occurs in approximately one to two cases per 1,000 births. Postpartum psychosis can cause extreme mood swings, delusions and confusion, according to the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada.

Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder, having plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the murders.

The trial, which is being held in Plymouth, Mass., is being livestreamed on CourtTV and major Boston TV stations, as well as YouTube. On Tuesday, the trial moved into day 11, and proceedings are expected to continue for several more weeks.

Here are some details about the case and what court has heard.

The killings

Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, was struggling with her mental health and seeing multiple specialists in 2022. The court has heard she was prescribed 13 different psychiatric medications across different providers.

Her attorneys say Clancy did everything she could to seek help: She turned to multiple outpatient providers, tried various drugs they prescribed, called a suicide hotline, went to an emergency room and approached but wasn’t accepted into a hospital-based, full-day treatment program for women with postpregnancy mental health problems. Clancy also checked herself into a psychiatric hospital for several days.

Rather than improving her condition, her attorneys and family say the shifting cocktail of psychiatric medications made things worse.

Cellphone records show that on Jan. 24, 2023, she texted her husband Patrick late in the afternoon, asking him to pick up takeout and medicine.

During his absence from their Duxbury, Mass., home, prosecutors say Clancy used exercise bands to strangle their three children: five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan. She then cut her own wrists and throat and jumped out of a second-storey window in an apparent suicide attempt.

Clancy, who turned 36 on Tuesday, was paralyzed from the waist down and has been attending the court proceedings in a wheelchair.

Court hears diary entries

Opening statements began on July 27, after an 18-member jury was selected.

Patrick Clancy, Lindsay's now former husband, took the stand early, detailing her mental health struggles and his experience on the day of the killings. Jurors were shaken when his 911 call was played in court.

The court later heard from Duxbury first responders, crime scene analysts and the family's nanny, who said Lindsay was a "wonderful mom who loved her kids."

Clancy's diary entries were also read in court, including a section where she wrote that she was “completely overwhelmed” trying to take care of her children.

“I feel like I’m drowning every day,” she wrote.

She sobbed in court when details of the autopsy reports were read.

Testimony from psychiatrists

Recent days have focused on Clancy's mental state, including testimonies from her psychiatrists and mental health experts.

On Monday her lawyer probed Dr. Jennifer Tufts, who saw Clancy via video meetings from September 2022 until the day before the killings.

Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington questioned Tufts' expertise, prescribing decisions and overall treatment, spotlighting her use of 25-minute video appointments and the series of recommended pharmaceuticals.

Defence attorney Kevin Reddington, left, questions psychiatrist Dr. Jennifer Tufts about her hand written notes on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

"I do not believe that I've been negligent," Tufts testified.

Clancy is suing Tufts and other practitioners in civil court.

On Tuesday, another of Clancy's psychiatrists, Rebecca Jollotta, testified about a concerning mid-December call with the couple during which she heard Clancy had her "worst day" and was "having persistent, intrusive thoughts of suicide."

Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham has urged jurors not to view the trial as "a public debate about women's mental health and how the medical system treats women," but rather to focus on the specific actions Clancy took and the intent behind them.

If convicted of murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole.

If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

Legal expert Margaret McLean told Parade that Clancy's case would then shift to a "civil commitment process" overseen by the court and mental health experts.

Clancy could eventually be released under strict conditions, or, if her illness is deemed "chronic and dangerous," she could remain institutionalized for the rest of her life.
