World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: YPF divests its stake in gas distribution for 780 million dollars
World.content:
YPF divests its stake in gas distribution for 780 million dollars

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 06:28 UTC Full article

YPF will transfer 70% of the capital of Metrogas, the country's largest gas distributor, and 5% of Metroenergía, its trading arm

Argentine oil company YPF, 51% state-controlled, has accepted Edenor's offer to buy its stake in Metrogas and Metroenergía for 780 million dollars, according to a filing submitted on Monday to the securities regulator. The deal takes the company out of the natural gas distribution business.

YPF will transfer 70% of the capital of Metrogas, the country's largest gas distributor, and 5% of Metroenergía, its trading arm. Metrogas supplies around 2.4 million customers in the city of Buenos Aires and eleven surrounding districts, more than a quarter of the national market. Edenor supplies electricity to 3.4 million customers in the northern part of the metropolitan area.

The buyer is controlled by the Edelcos consortium, made up of businessmen José Luis Manzano, Daniel Vila and Mauricio Filiberti. Manzano, a former interior minister under Carlos Menem, already held 9.23% of Metrogas through his investment vehicle. Once completed, the deal will place a single group in charge of the largest gas and electricity distributors in the metropolitan area, with close to 5.8 million customers combined.

The competitive process began in April with thirteen non-binding offers and narrowed to five finalists: besides Edenor, Central Puerto, MSU, Grupo Pierri and Litoral Gas took part. Citigroup advised the oil company. Edenor bid alongside British firm Andina PLC and will have to launch a tender offer for the remaining shares, held by the national social security administration, investors on the Buenos Aires stock exchange and Manzano's existing stake.

YPF said the sale forms part of a review of its asset portfolio and that proceeds will go to Vaca Muerta, the unconventional hydrocarbons field at the center of the strategy pursued by its chairman, Horacio Marín. Argentine law also bars vertical integration between gas production and distribution, an incompatibility the company had carried since taking control of Metrogas in 2012.

The timing coincides with improved results at the distributor. Between 2023 and 2025, Metrogas doubled its gross profit, quadrupled its operating result, cut its debt to a third and resumed dividend payments for the first time since 2001. The tariff adjustments introduced by Javier Milei's government and a five-year review setting an indexation formula shape the regulatory framework of the business.

Metrogas's licence, granted in 1992 for 35 years, expires in December 2027. The gas regulator has sent the executive a recommendation to extend it by two decades, to 2047, a decision not yet formalized. Completion of the transaction is conditional on authorizations from energy sector regulators.

World.title: Michelle and Flávio Bolsonaro appear together for the first time since their June rift
World.content:
Michelle and Flávio Bolsonaro appear together for the first time since their June rift

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 06:21 UTC Full article

“We have set our disagreements aside. What family is perfect? Let anyone without family problems raise their hand,” the former first lady said at the end of the event

Brazil's former first lady, Michelle Bolsonaro, and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate, appeared together in public on Tuesday for the first time since the falling-out between them in late June. The meeting took place at the party's headquarters in Brasília, where they recorded campaign material and prayed together.

“We have set our disagreements aside. What family is perfect? Let anyone without family problems raise their hand,” the former first lady said at the end of the event. She added that both had put their differences behind them to unite “in favor of something much greater,” and confirmed she will take part in the campaign. “He can count on me on social media and he can count on the strength of women spread across Brazil,” she said.

The dispute erupted in late June, when Michelle Bolsonaro released a video accusing her stepson of mistreating and humiliating her over internal party matters, leaving her support for his candidacy in doubt. “They treat me as if I were an idiot. As if I had arrived yesterday,” she said at the time. Flávio Bolsonaro posted an apology video in July inviting her to join the campaign, and she responded positively, although they had not appeared together in public until Tuesday.

The former first lady heads PL Mulher, the Liberal Party's women's wing, and her backing is considered significant among evangelical and female voters. On August 2 she was nominated as a Senate candidate for the Federal District, at a convention she was unable to attend because of a hospitalization; her brother read the speech she had prepared.

The reunion comes four days before the official start of campaigning for October's elections. Flávio Bolsonaro has not secured alliances with the parties of the so-called Centrão and is competing for conservative voters with former governor Ronaldo Caiado, governor Romeu Zema and political figure Renan Santos.

Polls differ in scale but agree in placing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking re-election, ahead. A Datafolha survey from mid-July gave him 48% against the senator's 43% in a potential runoff; later measurements cited by international agencies put the two at 44% and 39% respectively.

Jair Bolsonaro, Michelle's husband and Flávio's father, is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years for attempting a coup. He is barred from holding public office, has appealed the ruling and is seeking a legislative pardon.

Lula will open his campaign at the stadium in São Bernardo do Campo, in greater São Paulo, where he was a union leader. Flávio Bolsonaro will do so at Copacabana beach in Rio de Janeiro.

World.title: Argentina to mark every July 15 with the World Cup win that revived the Falklands dispute
World.content:
Argentina to mark every July 15 with the World Cup win that revived the Falklands dispute

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 06:13 UTC Full article

The decision was approved unanimously on August 5 at an executive committee meeting held at the association's Ezeiza complex

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) has established July 15 as National Football Teams Day, in tribute to the 2-1 win over England in the 2026 World Cup semi-final, the same match after which several players displayed a banner asserting a sovereignty claim over the Falklands that prompted a FIFA disciplinary case.

The decision was approved unanimously on August 5 at an executive committee meeting held at the association's Ezeiza complex. According to its statement, the date commemorates the “great and historic victory” of the side coached by Lionel Scaloni, which came from behind in Atlanta through goals by Enzo Fernández and Lautaro Martínez, both set up by Lionel Messi. The AFA specified that the recognition also covers all national teams — youth, men's and women's, futsal, beach football and field football — that train at the Lionel Andrés Messi complex. Argentina went on to lose the final to Spain.

After the final whistle on July 15, a group of players unfurled a sheet reading “Las Malvinas son argentinas” — “The Falklands are Argentine” — in front of the stands. The British government condemned the gesture and asked FIFA to investigate, considering it a political demonstration at an official competition. A spokesperson for then-prime minister Keir Starmer said, as reported by the Daily Mail, that “the World Cup might not be ours, the Falkland Islands definitely are”, adding that self-determination rests with the islanders.

FIFA rules prohibit political messaging at its competitions. The governing body's disciplinary committee opened proceedings against the AFA and several players, among them Giovani Lo Celso, Cristian Romero and Lisandro Martínez. The case remains open and no sanction has been decided. There is a precedent: FIFA had already begun proceedings over a similar banner displayed at a friendly against Bosnia in La Plata before the tournament.

Argentine President Javier Milei backed the players. He called the celebration “perfectly valid” and said it reflects a sentiment shared by Argentines, though he anticipated a fine from the governing body.

The AFA also said the banner will be handed to veterans of the Falklands War. It was made by a group of fans from a bedsheet and paint at a cost of under ten dollars, taken into the stadium without authorization and retrieved from the pitch by a member of the delegation's staff.

The United Kingdom has administered the Falklands since 1833. In the 2013 referendum, islanders voted overwhelmingly to retain their status as a British overseas territory. Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim over the islands.

World.title: US disables a Panama-flagged container ship off the coast of Pakistan
World.content:
US disables a Panama-flagged container ship off the coast of Pakistan

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 00:16 UTC Full article

A Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the vessel's engine room after its civilian crew ignored repeated warnings

US forces struck the Panama-flagged container ship Vela Nova in the Gulf of Oman on Tuesday, leaving it unable to steer, after it attempted to head for an Iranian port in violation of the naval blockade imposed by Washington, US Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed.

A Navy MH-60 helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles into the vessel's engine room after its civilian crew ignored repeated warnings, the command said in a statement. The strike disabled the ship's steering gear. A senior US official quoted earlier by The Wall Street Journal had said the shot was aimed at the rudder, and that the crew was subsequently transferred to another vessel.

The incident took place some 71 nautical miles — around 131 kilometers — off the coast of Pakistan, while the ship was sailing westbound. Maritime security firm Vanguard reported that the impact started a fire, later extinguished, and that all 17 crew members are safe. The British organization UKMTO had initially reported an incident involving a tanker.

The Panamanian flag corresponds to an open registry and does not imply any link to the Panamanian state or Panamanian ownership. Shipping records list Golden Valley Marine INV as registered owner and commercial manager, with Sino Hellenic Ships Management as technical manager and classification by the Korean Register.

It is the third vessel disabled since the United States reimposed the blockade on July 14. As of Tuesday, CENTCOM has redirected 55 commercial vessels attempting to cross the line, disabled three and boarded two, according to its own figures. The previous cases were the Curaçao-flagged Belma and the Mozambique-flagged Lavine, on July 24. In June, three Indian sailors died during a blockade enforcement operation, according to an Indian official at the time.

Charlie Brown, an adviser to the US organization United Against Nuclear Iran, told Reuters that the Vela Nova recently called at Mumbai and Port Klang, ports also used by vessels linked to Iran, and that the episode underscores the heightened scrutiny now being applied to Iran-related shipping.

The strike comes during a period of relative calm following the apparent collapse of the memorandum of understanding signed by the two countries in June and a thirteen-day escalation in July. Tehran and Washington exchanged mutual demands for compensation over war damage on Monday. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea.

World.title: Colombia asks for supplies but not foreign rescue personnel after the earthquake
World.content:
Colombia asks for supplies but not foreign rescue personnel after the earthquake

12th Wednesday, August 2026 - 00:05 UTC Full article

The Colombian government issued a diplomatic note on Tuesday requesting support from the international community with specific requirements

Colombia's government has requested international aid in the form of supplies for those affected by Monday's magnitude 7.4 earthquake, but has not called for foreign rescue teams, despite offers from at least six countries and multilateral bodies.

El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, was the one who made Colombia's position public. “The government of Colombia has requested humanitarian aid solely in the form of supplies to assist the families affected,” he wrote on social media. “We have been informed that its rescue teams, doctors and other emergency services are deployed and attending to the situation, so at this time they do not require personnel support.” El Salvador will send two cargo planes with a hundred tons of humanitarian aid.

Several governments have contingents on standby. Ecuador offered a search and rescue team of 47 personnel with specialized dogs and seven days of operational autonomy. Mexico assembled a unit with four tons of medicines and 8.4 tons of tools and rescue equipment, similar to the one deployed in Venezuela after June's earthquakes. “We are waiting for a formal request from the government of Colombia, but we are ready for the moment they tell us we can go and help,” President Claudia Sheinbaum said. Chile, Brazil, Peru, Guatemala and Spain, among others, also offered assistance.

The exception is the United States, which announced 15.5 million dollars in aid for emergency shelter, food, protection and damage assessment. The State Department said it activated a Disaster Assistance Response Team on Monday, due to arrive in the country on Tuesday.

The Colombian government issued a diplomatic note on Tuesday requesting support from the international community with specific requirements, a mechanism that does not formally amount to an international appeal. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said the organization remains in contact with the authorities and supports “the government-led response, as requested.” China's ambassador in Bogotá, Zhu Jingyang, called for a liaison official to be designated as soon as possible to coordinate assistance.

Colombia's emergency cooperation system is centralized in the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, which must set out requirements before the foreign ministry passes them to donors. “The government is learning on the go how the mechanism works,” said international relations scholar Sandra Borda, who added that cities cannot channel aid directly. President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on August 7, announced the appointment of geological engineer David Suárez Tamayo to head the unit.

World.title: At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia
World.content:
At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:51 UTC Full article

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead

At least 132 people were killed and 570 injured by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday, according to the latest report submitted by the Colombian Association of Capital Cities at 7:00 p.m. local time. Authorities warned the figure is preliminary and that rescue work is continuing.

The quake struck at 07:34, with its epicenter near the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, at a depth of more than 80 kilometers, according to the Colombian Geological Service. It is the strongest recorded in the country in the past decade.

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead. Departmental tolls released by governors and mayors correspond to different cutoff times and do not match one another: Chocó governor Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi reported 12 dead and 84 injured in that department, while the mayor of Manizales confirmed two deaths. Fatalities were also reported in Valle del Cauca and Antioquia.

| URGENTE: Momento del derrumbe de un edificio de 3 pisos tras el terremoto de magnitud 7,4 en Pereira, Colombia. pic.twitter.com/r3v2lW5pU3 — Alerta News 24 (@AlertaNews24) August 10, 2026

The government put the number of damaged homes at more than 1,500, with 37 destroyed and 61 buildings completely collapsed, along with damage to 18 health centers, 52 schools, 17 community centers and 18 roads. The civil aviation authority suspended operations at seven air terminals: Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.

Damage to the hospital network is among the most critical. In Cali, the Hospital Universitario del Valle partially collapsed and seven large health care institutions were closed and evacuated because of structural damage. Valle del Cauca governor Dilian Francisca Toro said at least five intensive care patients were trapped under rubble. Cali mayor Alejandro Eder reported at least twenty collapsed structures with people trapped inside and requested rescue teams from Bogotá and Medellín. The capital's mayor, Carlos Fernando Galán, dispatched a hundred rescue workers.

De la Espriella agreed to declare a national disaster situation and is leading a unified command post at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, with additional posts in Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry is coordinating international cooperation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was ready to provide assistance.

The Colombian Geological Service reported two aftershocks, of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8. The agency also recorded an emission of ash and gases from the Puracé volcano, in Cauca department, on orange alert since July, coinciding in time with the earthquake.

World.title: Colombia and Venezuela quakes are unconnected despite similar magnitude, experts say
World.content:
Colombia and Venezuela quakes are unconnected despite similar magnitude, experts say

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:11 UTC Full article

“The Venezuelan earthquakes are shallower and involve a different mechanism, a strike-slip mechanism. This one is deeper, a subduction earthquake,” a seismologist stressed

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday has a different tectonic origin from the earthquakes recorded in Venezuela in June, despite comparable magnitudes, said Viviana Dionisio, a seismologist with Colombia's National Seismological Network.

“It was a tectonic earthquake associated mainly with a subduction mechanism,” the specialist said. That process occurs when the Nazca plate, beneath the Pacific Ocean, slides under the South American plate, on which Colombia's mainland territory sits. Energy accumulated at the contact between the two can be released in large earthquakes, of the kind historically recorded around the Pacific Ring of Fire.

The Venezuelan earthquakes of June 24, of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.4, responded to a different mechanism. According to Dionisio, they originated in the interaction between the Caribbean and South American plates through lateral displacement, known as strike-slip faulting. “The Venezuelan earthquakes are shallower and involve a different mechanism, a strike-slip mechanism. This one is deeper, a subduction earthquake,” she stressed.

Depth is the factor explaining why two earthquakes of similar magnitude can cause very different damage. The focus of the Colombian quake was located at around one hundred kilometers, according to revised data from the Colombian Geological Service, which in its first bulletin had placed it at 82. In shallow earthquakes, waves travel a shorter distance and reach areas near the epicenter with greater intensity; in deep ones they pass through more material and lose energy along the way. The seismologist warned, however, that depth alone does not determine the extent of damage, which also depends on the vulnerability of buildings and ground conditions.

The epicenter was located in San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, on the boundary with Risaralda and Valle del Cauca. Dionisio said it is not unusual for an earthquake of these characteristics to originate in that region, given the tectonic dynamics of western Colombia.

The Colombian Geological Service has recorded more than thirty aftershocks, the strongest of magnitude 4.8. “An earthquake of this magnitude generates a certain number of aftershocks that generally decrease in frequency and magnitude over the following days or weeks,” the seismologist said.

Rodrigo León, of the Geosciences Department at Universidad de los Andes, noted that earthquakes cannot be predicted, nor is it possible to anticipate when an aftershock will occur or to rule out larger movements. He also considered that, given the magnitude of the event, the damage could have been worse. The provisional toll exceeds 130 dead.

World.title: American Airlines resumes its seasonal Montevideo-Miami route in December
World.content:
American Airlines resumes its seasonal Montevideo-Miami route in December

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:00 UTC Full article

The operation is not the restoration of a discontinued route but the reopening of a service the company suspends each year outside the tourist season

American Airlines will restart its seasonal service between Carrasco International Airport and Miami International Airport on December 3, once again becoming the only carrier offering nonstop flights between Uruguay and the United States during the peak summer season.

The operation is not the restoration of a discontinued route but the reopening of a service the company suspends each year outside the tourist season. The change from the previous cycle is the extension of the daily-frequency stretch: in 2025-2026 daily flights ran until February 11, while this season they will continue until March 2, 2027, some three weeks longer.

From that date, the connection will operate three times a week, on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays, until March 28, 2027, when the scheduled season ends.

The route will be flown by a Boeing 787-8 with capacity for 234 passengers, in a configuration of 20 Business class seats, 28 in Premium Economy and 186 in the main cabin. According to the itinerary released by the airline, flights from Miami will depart at 22:55 and arrive in Montevideo at 10:10 the following day. In the opposite direction, departures from Carrasco are set for 22:30, landing in Miami at 05:45. Times are local and subject to change. The journey takes approximately nine hours.

“After nearly three decades of dedicated service to Uruguay, we are delighted to resume our daily seasonal flights in Montevideo for the busiest period of the summer,” said Pascual Álvarez, the company's managing director of operations for South America, Central America and the Caribbean. He said the route targets both international travelers visiting Uruguay and Uruguayan passengers connecting from Miami to other destinations.

Miami is the airline's main international connecting hub, with more than 400 daily flights in peak season to over 200 destinations, according to company figures.

At Aeropuertos Uruguay, the concession holder for the Carrasco terminal, commercial director Matías Carluccio said the reactivation “strengthens Uruguay's access to the United States and broadens travel options for passengers seeking to connect our country with new international destinations.” He added that the company would continue working to support the growth of air connectivity.

American Airlines has operated in Uruguay for close to thirty years. The Miami connection is the only direct route between the South American country and US territory, and its calendar coincides with the busiest tourist season in the River Plate.

World.title: Made in Mexico: Why UNAM is more than a university
World.content:
Listen to this article

As 58,000 university applicants sit a rerun of an entrance exam this month, it’s worth asking where exactly they are competing to enter. Their goal, the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), is an institution with 475 years of history, a campus built on a lava field, and a claim on Mexican public life that no other university comes close to.

Between Aug. 12 and 19, tens of thousands of Mexican teenagers are filing into convention centers in León, Oaxaca, Tijuana and Mexico City to take an entrance exam most of them had already passed. UNAM ran its undergraduate admissions test entirely online for the first time this year, with AI-supervised proctoring.

It did not hold. Some 2% of exams were annulled outright, score distributions looked nothing like the previous five years, enrollment was frozen across every degree program, and a technical commission recommended that a large slice of the applicant pool prove their results again, in person, with human invigilators watching.

That a single university can pause its own school year and hold the country’s attention for a month is itself the story. Here is why it can.

A university older than the country

On Sept. 21, 1551, Charles V signed a decree creating the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico. Classes began in January 1553 in a building near the Zócalo, with a faculty teaching theology, canon law, arts and medicine to the sons of the colonial elite. It was among the first universities in the Americas, founded the same year as San Marcos in Lima, and for nearly three centuries it produced the priests, jurists and administrators who ran New Spain.

Independence nearly finished it. To 19th-century liberals, a scholastic institution licensed by the Spanish Crown and blessed by the Pope was precisely the sort of thing a modern republic should dismantle.

So the university was closed, reopened, closed again — four or five times, depending on how you count — until it was shut for good in the 1860s and stayed shut for the better part of half a century. What survived in the gap were the professional schools that had spun off from it: jurisprudence, medicine, engineering, fine arts. In 1867, Gabino Barreda added the Escuela Nacional Preparatoria, which trained generations of Mexicans to think of science as a civic project.

The university came back on Sept. 22, 1910, as one of the last acts of the Porfiriato. Justo Sierra, education minister under then-President Porfirio Díaz, gathered the scattered schools into a National University of Mexico and added a School of Higher Studies for research and graduate work. In his inaugural address, he made a point of insisting the new institution was not the heir of the colonial one — that it had no pedigree, only a mandate to serve the nation. Six weeks later the Revolution began.

What followed is a long argument about independence. Students went on strike in 1929, and the government of Emilio Portes Gil granted the university autonomy: the right to name its own authorities, set its own curricula and manage its own budget without the president’s approval. That is when the “A” entered the acronym.

The 1945 Organic Law, still in force, locked the arrangement in place. Autonomy has been tested by nearly every administration since, and it has held — imperfectly, noisily, but it has held.

The shield and motto came from José Vasconcelos, rector in 1920–21, who put an Aztec eagle and an Andean condor over a map of Latin America and wrote beneath them “Por mi raza hablará el espíritu,” or “The spirit will speak for my race.”

The city on the lava

By the 1940s, the university was bursting out of roughly 40 buildings scattered across the historic center. The site chosen for a purpose-built campus was, by any conventional measure, absurd: the Pedregal de San Ángel, a black basalt wasteland in the south of the city laid down when the Xitle volcano erupted around 280 CE. The same lava had buried the pyramid at Cuicuilco, a few hundred meters away. Nothing had been built there in 17 centuries.

That was rather the point. Construction ran from 1950 to 1952 under Mario Pani and Enrique del Moral, with Carlos Lazo managing the works and more than 50 architects, engineers and artists involved — Luis Barragán and Pedro Ramírez Vázquez among them. Rather than clear the rock, they built around it, letting the lava run between the buildings and using volcanic stone in the walls.

Two hundred and thirty-seven hectares of the Pedregal survive inside the campus today as an ecological reserve, one of the last fragments of the ecosystem that once covered the southern valley.

The organizing idea was integración plástica: architecture, engineering, landscape and monumental art conceived as a single work rather than decorated after the fact.

There are roughly 110 murals on campus. Juan O’Gorman covered all four windowless faces of the Central Library with a mosaic assembled from natural colored stone he collected from across the country — no pigment, just rock — depicting the pre-Hispanic past, the colonial period, the modern world and the university itself. Siqueiros worked the Rectoría tower in relief that changes as you walk past it. Diego Rivera left a high-relief mosaic on the Olympic Stadium, unfinished. Francisco Eppens did Medicine, José Chávez Morado the Alfonso Caso auditorium.

Ciudad Universitaria was dedicated in November 1952 and occupied in 1954. In 2007, UNESCO inscribed the central campus on the World Heritage list — 176.5 hectares of the 730 — calling it one of the defining symbols of modernity in Latin America. Its stadium hosted the opening ceremony of the 1968 Olympics.

What it has meant

Which brings us to the more interesting question: what a university this size actually does to a country.

In 1935, Mexico had almost no doctors outside its cities. Gustavo Baz Prada, then director of the School of Medicine, told his graduating students that instead of collecting their degrees they would spend six months in towns without physicians, on a government stipend of 90 pesos a month, working as doctor and sanitation officer at once.

The experiment became mandatory social service for every UNAM student within two years, was written into Article 5 of the Constitution in 1942, and remains a graduation requirement at every university in the country. It is arguably the most consequential policy the institution ever exported.

Then there is 1968. When riot police blew open the 18th-century door of the Escuela Nacional Preparatoria with a bazooka that July, Rector Javier Barros Sierra lowered the university flag to half-staff and, on Aug. 1, led a march down Insurgentes at the head of his own students.

The army occupied Ciudad Universitaria on Sept. 18. Two weeks after that came Tlatelolco: on Oct. 2, 10 days before the Olympic flame arrived at the university’s own stadium, troops opened fire on a student rally in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas. The death toll has never been settled — official counts at the time ran to a few dozen, independent estimates into the hundreds.

In 1985, student brigades were among the first into the rubble after the earthquake; the seismological service that still warns the city when the ground moves is run out of the Institute of Geophysics. Between 1999 and 2000, a proposal to charge modest tuition triggered a strike that closed the campus for nearly 10 months, and ended with federal police walking onto it. Tuition remained free. No rector has proposed changing that since.

The alumni list runs to all three Mexican Nobel laureates. Alfonso García Robles (Peace, 1982) studied law in the old Escuela de Jurisprudencia and went on to negotiate the Treaty of Tlatelolco, which kept nuclear weapons out of Latin America. Octavio Paz (Literature, 1990) enrolled in law and letters and left without finishing. Mario Molina (Chemistry, 1995) took a chemical engineering degree before the work on CFCs that produced the Montreal Protocol.

President Claudia Sheinbaum did her physics degree at the Faculty of Sciences, as well as her doctorate in energy engineering. She was also a researcher at the Institute of Engineering — as were, in one faculty or another, most of her predecessors and a large share of the country’s judges, novelists, epidemiologists and cabinet ministers.

Today, some 380,000 students are enrolled, from junior high through doctoral programs, and tuition is effectively free. Which is why the exam matters.

This year UNAM will admit around 50,000 first-year undergraduates, more than half of them automatically from its own high schools. That leaves roughly 22,000 places for the 158,727 people who sat the test — an admission rate near 14%. Classes for the incoming class begin Aug. 31, two weeks late.

The institution will absorb this the way it has absorbed closure, occupation and strike. The applicants have rather less margin.

Maria Meléndez writes for Mexico News Daily in Mexico City.

World.title: Is Mexico ‘next’? Why Colombia’s deadly quake doesn’t raise the seismic odds here
World.content:
This week’s powerful earthquake in Colombia has revived fear in Mexico: Is the Pacific Ring of Fire about to send another major tremor north?

The answer is no. Although Mexico faces real seismic risk, Monday’s 7.4-magnitude quake in western Colombia is not a scientific warning that Mexico is next.

Colombia’s Geological Service said the quake was the country’s strongest of the 21st century. The death toll had risen above 200 by Tuesday as rescue operations continued, Reuters reported.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has pledged “all the support” Colombia needs, depending on a formal request from Colombian authorities.

The Venezuelan state news outlet Telesur reported Tuesday that Mexico is prepared to deploy a 255-member military search-and-rescue team, along with satellite phones, radios, electric generators, tents, four tons of medicines, 8.4 tons of tools and rescue equipment, 8,798 food packages and 13,890 food baskets.

Mexico and Colombia sit on the vast belt of faults, volcanoes and subduction zones that partly encircles the Pacific Ocean. The Cinturón de Fuego del Pacífic, or Pacific Ring of Fire, stretches about 40,000 kilometers from New Zealand through Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan; across the Aleutian Islands; and down the Pacific coasts of the Americas to Chile.

It is associated with roughly 90% of the world’s earthquakes and three-quarters of its active volcanoes.

But a shared belt does not make the two countries part of one seismic domino line.

In Colombia, seismic and volcanic activity reflects the interaction of the Nazca, South American and Caribbean plates.

Monday’s quake was linked principally to the Nazca-South American plate system.

Mexico’s principal Pacific-coast hazard comes from the Cocos Plate pushing beneath the North American Plate; the Rivera Plate is also a factor in the west. That configuration drives Mexico’s seismicity and volcanic systems.

Scientists know that seismic waves from a major earthquake can sometimes disturb faults far from the epicenter, a phenomenon known as dynamic triggering. But that possibility does not allow them to forecast a destructive earthquake in Mexico.

Likewise, a series of earthquakes across Latin America does not mean the Pacific Ring of Fire has been “activated.” Plates are always moving, accumulating and releasing stress along separate faults at different depths.

With reports from El Financiero, Infobae, WRadio and La Razón de México

World.title: Supply-demand squeeze could push Mexico home prices up 8% by the end of 2026
World.content:
Home prices in Mexico could increase by as much as 7% to 8% by the end of 2026, according to Fitch Ratings’ most recent Global Housing and Mortgage Outlook (GHMO) 2026, driven by a persistent imbalance between limited housing supply and resilient demand.

The GHMO cited high construction costs as restricting the development of new projects. Meanwhile, mortgage rates remain at historically high levels, restricting borrowers’ access to credit.

According to the Federal Mortgage Society, the national housing price index increased by 8.7% in the first quarter of 2026 and 7.3% in the second quarter (compared to the same periods of last year), with cumulative growth for the first half of the year coming in at 7.9%. This remains lower than the historical highs of 10.4% and 10.06% recorded in 2022 and 2023, respectively.

In the first half of the year, single-family homes appreciated by 8.4%, while the combined price increase of condominiums and apartments was 7.4%.

Public or subsidized housing increased in value by 10% and middle-income housing appreciated by 6.7%.

During this period, the national average home value was 1,960,032 pesos (US $114,709), with 75% of homes valued below 2,226,101 pesos ($130,289).

By metropolitan area, Guadalajara experienced the highest housing price increase, at 11%, followed by Monterrey, 8.3%, and Puebla-Tlaxcala, 8.5%.

By state, Tamaulipas experienced the greatest increase, at 11.8%, followed by Quintana Roo at 11.5% and Jalisco at 11.2%.

CDMX rental prices

The Mexico City government announced plans earlier in the year to prohibit rent increases beyond the previous year’s inflation rate, as well as expand the social housing stock.

Average rent in the capital has increased by 9.6% year-on-year, over three times the current inflation rate. The highest rents are concentrated in the boroughs of Cuauhtémoc and Miguel Hidalgo, and the neighbourhoods of Hipódromo Condesa, Juárez and San Rafael.

Improvements made in the city for the hosting of the 2026 FIFA World Cup have driven up prices in some areas.

The average cost of a two-bedroom, 65-square-meter apartment was 21,921 pesos ($1,283) per month, equivalent to almost 70 days of minimum wage, while a three-bedroom, 100-square-meter apartment stood at 30,618 pesos ($1,792), or more than 97 days, according to data from the Inmuebles24 real estate listings platform.

With reports from La Jornada and Informador

World.title: Mexico seeks bids for 5G telecom system on 2 new passenger train lines
World.content:
The federal Ministry of Infrastructure, Communications and Transport (SICT) last week launched an international tender to select a company to design, install and maintain a 5G telecommunications network for two passenger rail corridors that are currently under construction.

In an Aug. 6 statement, SICT said that via the Integrated Trains and Public Transport Agency (Attrapi), it issued an “international public call for bids for the design, supply, installation, commissioning, and maintenance of the telecommunications network on the Mexico City–Querétaro–Irapuato and Saltillo–Nuevo Laredo rail sections.”

“… The telecommunications network that is the subject of the tender includes 5G Standalone Railroad Radio Communications, a state-of-the-art mobile communication system with advanced signaling and train safety [features],” the ministry said.

Such a network allows trains to communicate with each other and rail control centers, making it essential to the safe operation of railroads.

The construction of the Mexico City–Querétaro–Irapuato and Saltillo–Nuevo Laredo rail corridors is part of an ambitious plan to significantly increase Mexico’s passenger railroad network. Various new lines are slated to open in the coming years. In its 2026 budget, the federal government allocated more than 104 billion pesos (US $6.1 billion) to new rail projects.

SICT said that proposals for the design and installation of the 5G network for the Mexico City–Querétaro–Irapuato and Saltillo–Nuevo Laredo train lines will be accepted from Sept. 14, with a decision to be announced on Sept. 25. Proposals must be in Spanish with costings in Mexican pesos.

According to Attrapi, the estimated commencement date for the telecommunications network project is Oct. 1, 2026.

SICT noted that the call for bids specifies that there will be no site visit due to “the project’s geographic scope.”

“The [two] railway sections under construction measure 675 kilometers,” the ministry said, noting also that the call for bids was published in the Official Gazette of the Federation.

With reports from Expansión

World.title: Tulum regains 5 lost international air routes, a hopeful sign for tourism sector recovery
World.content:
Tulum’s Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport will regain five international connections during the 2026–2027 winter season, a sign of recovery from the destination’s tourism decline.

Operations will begin in late October this year and continue through March 2027.

According to an announcement from Quintana Roo Governor Mara Lezama, Tulum will be receiving international flights of varying frequencies throughout the winter from four strategic Canadian cities — Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Quebec — and five from the U.S., including Newark, Houston, Dallas, Miami and Atlanta. Some of those routes are already active and others will soon begin operating.

The expansion of air service is part of the Tulum Renace (Rebirth of Tulum) program, a federal strategy aimed at reorganizing the destination, strengthening its infrastructure and attracting a greater influx of high-value tourists to tackle its ongoing slump in tourism since last year.

Reports from July revealed that the Tulum airport saw its international routes drop from 12 to four this year, alongside a decline of more than 30% in international traffic.

Quintana Roo’s Tourism Minister Bernardo Cueto told the specialized news outlet Aviación Online that the decline in operations is not an isolated phenomenon, but one that is replicated in destinations across Mexico, the Caribbean and the U.S., where airlines have chosen to prioritize maintaining existing routes over opening new markets.

On the other hand, the competing destination of Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic mobilized at its airport over 11 million passengers in 2025, compared to the 1.2 million travelers Tulum’s airport handled in the same period.

To boost Tulum’s tourism industry, the state government is also launching an aggressive three-year incentive plan to bring back other airlines that suspended operations and attract new direct flights from the U.S., Germany and Panama.

The incentives include financial support and operational accommodations to reduce financial risk for airlines and encourage their immediate return.

“We want airlines to see Tulum as a real and profitable opportunity,” Cueto said.

With reports from El Economista, Novedades Quintana Roo, El Quintanarroense

World.title: Mexico’s formal sector is posting gains in employment and pay, even as World Cup hangover hits
World.content:
Mexico lost more formal sector jobs last month than in any July on record.

The Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) reported on Monday that the number of people in formal sector jobs declined by 19,550 in July compared to the previous month. On a month-over-month basis, the workforce shrank by 0.1%.

“This result reflects, among other factors, seasonality associated with the end of the school year and, in part, the declining phase of the agricultural cycle,” IMSS said in a statement.

However, data shows that the size of Mexico’s formal sector workforce usually increases in July.

In a period of almost three decades dating back to 1998 — when IMSS first kept comparable records — Mexico has lost formal sector jobs in July in just six years, while the workforce increased in the seventh month of 23 years.

So what was the real reason for the record job losses last month? The conclusion of the FIFA men’s World Cup, suggests a report by the news outlet Bloomberg Línea.

“After the final whistle of the 2026 World Cup, Mexico lost more formal jobs in July than had ever been recorded in official records,” Bloomberg Línea reported.

The loss of almost 20,000 formal sector jobs in July came after Mexico’s formal workforce grew by 61,023 positions in June, the month in which Mexico hosted 12 of its 13 World Cup matches. The final World Cup match in Mexico was the July 5 round of 16 clash between Mexico and England in Mexico City.

In addition to the creation of employment directly related to the World Cup, such as jobs in stadiums, the increase in June was attributed to growth in the size of the workforce of drivers for ridesharing companies such as Uber and Didi. Demand for ridesharing services increased during the World Cup, particularly in the Mexico City metropolitan area.

The launch of a program that provides employment benefits to digital platform workers has helped prop up Mexico’s formal sector job numbers since last year. According to an analysis by Manpower Group, a staffing company, Mexico would have lost 29,823 jobs in July if 10,273 digital platform workers hadn’t entered the formal workforce.

Alberto Alesi, Manpower Group’s general director in Mexico, said that companies are currently demonstrating a high degree of caution when it comes to hiring.

“Economic challenges are the primary factor driving caution and potential workforce reductions, and they will be decisive in determining the net increase in formal jobs by the end of 2026,” he said.

IMSS also reported on Monday that the number of formal sector employers declined on a month-over-month and annual basis in July. At the end of last month, 1.01 million employers were affiliated with IMSS, down 0.2% compared to June and 2.5% on an annual basis.

The month-over-month decline in July in the size of Mexico’s formal sector workforce and in the number of employers came after the Mexican economy, buoyed by World Cup spending, grew 1.5% on a sequential basis in the second quarter of 2026, according to preliminary data. The economy contracted 0.6% on a sequential basis in the first quarter of the year.

Mexico has added more than 243,000 formal sector jobs this year

IMSS data shows that 22.76 million people were in IMSS-affiliated formal sector jobs at the end of July.

The institute said that is the fourth-highest figure on record and the highest for any July.

IMSS said that 87% of formal sector workers are in permanent positions while the remaining 13% are in temporary jobs.

In the first seven months of 2026, Mexico’s formal sector workforce grew by 243,078 positions, according to IMSS. Over 95% of the new jobs are permanent positions, IMSS said. The increase in formal sector jobs in the first seven months of this year is 24.8% higher than in the same period of last year.

The total number of formal sector jobs increased on a month-over-month basis in February, March, April and June, and declined in January, May and July. The largest number of job losses in a single month this year occurred in May, when the formal sector workforce shrank by more than 29,000 positions.

In the 12 months to the end of July, Mexico added 326,987 formal sector jobs, representing annual growth of 1.5%.

While Mexico’s formal sector is growing, the majority of Mexican workers continue to toil in the country’s vast informal sector. In June, 55% of all Mexican workers were employed in the informal sector, according to the national statistics agency INEGI.

Baja California and Oaxaca lead Mexico for annual job growth

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, the northern state of Baja California recorded the highest annual formal sector job growth in July. That state’s formal sector workforce grew 7% in the 12 months to July 31.

Oaxaca recorded the second strongest annual growth. The southern state’s formal sector workforce grew 5.8% in the 12 months to the end of July.

Six other states recorded annual job growth above 3%. They were México state (3.8%); San Luis Potosí (3.6%); Tabasco (3.5%); Hidalgo (3.5%); Durango (3.5%); and Mexico City (3.3%).

All told, the formal sector workforces of 19 entities increased in the 12 months to the end of July, while 13 entities lost jobs in the period.

The largest contraction occurred in the Gulf coast state of Campeche, whose formal sector workforce decreased by 7.3% in the 12 months to the end of July. The next biggest contractions occurred in Tamaulipas (-2.5%); Quintana Roo (2.4%); and Morelos (2.4%). Among the other entities that lost formal sector jobs over the past year was the violence-plagued state of Sinaloa.

Transport and communications sector records strongest job growth

IMSS data also shows that the workforce in Mexico’s transport and communications sector increased by 7.5% in the 12 months to the end of July.

The mining sector recorded the second strongest annual job growth (+4.3%), followed by social services (+3.3%), electricity (+2.1%), services for companies (1.8%), commerce (+1.7%) and construction (+1.2%).

Meanwhile, the workforce of the transformation (manufacturing) sector shrank 0.7% in the 12 months to the end of July, while the number of people employed in the agriculture sector declined 5.6%.

Mexico’s average formal sector salary reaches a record high

IMSS reported that the average daily base salary for an IMSS-affiliated formal sector worker at the end of July was 673.9 pesos (US $39.40), an annual increase of 42.4 pesos or 6.7%.

IMSS said that the average formal sector salary in July was the highest on record.

With reports from Bloomberg Línea, EFE, Expansión and El Economista

World.title: Attacks by and towards crocodiles are on the rise in Puerto Vallarta
World.content:
The deaths of 11 crocodiles in Puerto Vallarta over the past several weeks have prompted Jalisco state environmental officials to issue a plea for greater respect for wildlife.

At the same time, authorities are publicizing cautionary strategies to prevent encounters with the reptiles that could be dangerous, even lethal, to humans. The concern has grown since a Mexico City tourist was killed by a crocodile on a Puerto Vallarta beach in late June.

The American crocodile (Crocodylus acutus) is listed under special protection according to federal environmental laws due to its key role in the ecological balance of estuaries, wetlands and rivers.

Officials acknowledge that there has been a marked recent increase in sightings and interactions between people and crocodiles. But the state Ministry of Environment and Territorial Development (Semadet) insists that it is not due to overpopulation of the species.

The total population of crocodiles in the Banderas Bay area (which straddles Jalisco and the state of Nayarit to the north and includes Puerto Vallarta) is estimated at between 300 and 350.

Instead, Semadet said that during the rainy season crocodiles typically increase their movements between estuaries, rivers and the sea, resulting in greater visibility as well as the likelihood of increased interruption of human activities.

Semadet will continue the installation and standardization of preventive signage in areas considered to have greater possibilities of interaction, particularly at deltas and estuaries.

The Puerto Vallarta government has reinforced surveillance operations in these areas, placing warning flags and providing escorts for large crocodiles, in order to prevent risks to tourists and residents.

What to do if you encounter a crocodile

Semadet, which last year introduced a bilingual strategy for responsible coexistence between humans and crocodiles, issued a reminder that if you encounter a crocodile, the most important thing is to remain calm and immediately increase the distance to at least 25 meters:

Walk away slowly, without sudden movements and avoid making noise that might attract the animal’s attention.

If the animal starts to approach or displays aggressive behavior, quickly move away, remembering to run in a straight line and away from the water.

Never try to approach, touch, feed, or scare it away on your own. As soon as you are in a safe place, warn others and report the sighting to Civil Protection or emergency services.

Obey all warning signs and do not approach bodies of water where so advised. Keep in mind that you should not allow dogs or other animals near bodies of water where a crocodile may be found.

With reports from Informador, N+ and Quadratín Jalisco

World.title: MND Local: Tijuana Innovadora and upcoming events in Baja California
World.content:
When businessman José Galicot Behar founded Tijuana Innovadora in 2010, the goal was to help change the narrative about the city, focusing not on crime, but rather on the city’s growing status as a business capital. In the 16 years since the first event at the Centro Cultural Tijuana (CECUT), that’s exactly what has happened — as Tijuana Innovadora has evolved from a biennial event to a continuous, year-round civic movement, with an increasing list of actionable results to its credit.

A pollution monitoring program for the Tijuana River

Toxic waste and raw sewage polluting the Tijuana River have long been an issue affecting residents on both sides of the border, and a bone of contention between the U.S. and Mexico. An estimated 35 million to 50 million gallons of contaminated water flow through the river daily, with significant impacts for local beaches and border ecosystems. The two nations signed an agreement in 2025 aimed at helping to clean up the issue, with US $93 million earmarked for infrastructure projects. But it’s not just the governments who are working to find solutions.

Tijuana Innovadora has recently announced its participation in the Río Tijuana Initiative, which brings together a binational group of 24 representatives from Mexico and the United States to establish a baseline of water quality. Trained volunteers and students, known as “River Sentinels,” will collect samples at 10 points along the channel as part of a campaign scheduled for this month. The program will measure eight water-quality parameters to identify pollution hotspots and assess their severity.

Samples will be processed in the Biotechnology Engineering laboratories at the Tijuana Institute of Technology, giving the findings an academic basis. The results will then feed into the Tijuana River Index, a platform designed to translate complex data and provide a tangible basis for measuring future outcomes.

A promotional platform to drive medical and dental tourism

Tijuana Innovadora has also joined forces with the Baja Health Cluster, a regional industry association, to help promote medical and dental tourism in Baja California.

The new agreement, announced last month at the CODET Vision Institute, is not about building hospitals or providing medical care. Tijuana Innovadora’s plan is simply to help showcase the state’s high-quality medical services and share the merits of the region’s doctors, clinics, hospitals and health workers.

Tijuana, in particular, is among the most popular medical tourism destinations in Mexico and a leader in an industry that in 2024 brought in over US $2 billion in revenue to the state. Only Sonora among Mexican states outpaces Baja California when it comes to medical tourism. However, the number of visitors was down significantly in Baja California in 2025, so an increased emphasis on promotional efforts does seem to be warranted.

As MND reported in June, the dental tourism market in Mexico is expected to quadruple over the next eight years — growing from US $527 million in 2025 to US $2.2 billion by 2033 — with Tijuana and Baja California poised to be key beneficiaries. So here, too, promotion could be an important tool in highlighting available regional services.

Fiestas de la Vendimia 2026

In terms of economic impact, no summer event in Baja California compares to Fiestas de la Vendimia, the monthlong wine harvest festival held primarily in Valle de Guadalupe, but with events also taking place in Ensenada and Tijuana. Over 90,000 visitors are expected at the 36th annual iteration of the event, slated for Aug. 5-30, 2026, with the economic value estimated at over 600 million pesos.

Among the 35 events scheduled over 25 days this month by Provino — the local non-profit winegrowers association — are tastings, pairing dinners, concerts and other experiences, including the traditional cooking contest, Concurso de Paellas. Over 80 wineries are expected to participate during this year’s festivities, which spotlights viticulture in Mexico’s most famous and productive wine region, with the state accounting for about 70% of all wine produced in the country.

Feria Nacional de Tijuana 2026

Aficionados of regional parties can also look forward to the upcoming Feria Nacional de Tijuana, an outgrowth of the previous Feria de las Californias that offers rides, regional food and culture, plus concerts featuring some of the best-known performers in Mexico at venues in Parque Morelos. This year’s event runs from Aug. 28 to Sept. 27, as part of celebrations surrounding Mexico’s Independence Day.

Access to musical performances in the open-air Teatro del Pueblo is typically included with general admission prices, while premium tickets are required to see acts like the acclaimed norteño band Los Tucanes de Tijuana (Friday, Sept. 4 at 8 p.m.) at the park’s Palenque concert arena.

Recapping Opera en la Calle 2026

Although the season’s biggest events still lie ahead, one long-time favorite has already wrapped up its 2026 edition: Opera en la Calle, a Tijuana summer institution since 2004. At its outset, the goal was to make opera and classical music more accessible to the general public through performances from talented artists. That goal has certainly been accomplished, as an estimated quarter of a million people attended the annual fête during its first two decades of operation.

This year’s free event, the 23rd annual, was held on Saturday, July 18, with approximately 300 artists and 100 support staff putting on a show for approximately 8,700 attendees during 10-plus hours of programming on Calle 11, between Avenida Revolución and Avenida Madero.

Like Tijuana Innovadora, the Feria Nacional de Tijuana and the Fiestas de la Vendimia, it’s one of the things that makes summertime special in Baja California.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: The Cheap Drone Problem: The Infrastructure Bill Latin America Hasn’t Costed Yet
World.content:
Analysis · Security

Key Facts — Leipzig/Halle Explosive-laden drone found on Aug 5, 2026, defused by robot

— Germany Over 1,000 suspicious drone flights logged in 2025

— Frankfurt 45 sightings in 11 months, up from 17 the year before (~165% rise)

— Berlin Federal police assign ~130 officers to drone defence unit with jammers and interceptors

— Europe Aéroports de Lyon deploys Ascento Guard patrol robots in car parks

— LatAm Brazil, Mexico, Argentina named in airport security robotics market reports

— Covered List FCC adds foreign-made advanced robots on July 28, 2026, shaping supplier choices

— Vendors Smiths Detection, Leidos, Teledyne, Atmosic among major airport security firms

Europe is building a counter-drone playbook. Latin America’s ports, mines, and airports face the same threat, and the bill is coming due.

The Cheap Drone Problem: The Infrastructure Bill Latin America Hasn’t Costed Yet. (Photo internet reproduction)
